Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva—this is a phrase of true and direct speech. Every person possesses this Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva;

it is only because of the obstructions of the six sense faculties and their various objects that one is unable to perceive it. Being pulled by the myriad conditions of emotional desires, one fails to attain mastery.

If there is a person of wisdom who attains faith and can let go, they need only choose a secluded and quiet place to settle the body and mind, sitting until they reach the utmost stillness—stillness within stillness, free from even the slightest heterodox thought. With a single, pure mind, maintain this ultimate tranquility;
then, with a sudden movement, a True Person will appear within one’s own spiritual palace, coming and going as they please.
Transcending both the vertical and the horizontal, there is nothing to be attained. Only here do you truly see your own Bodhisattva, wandering at ease and with sovereign freedom.
In a single kṣaṇa, they pervade the entire realm of sands; all are living Bodhisattvas, their radiance shining everywhere.
If you wish to see this Bodhisattva, do not use your eyes to observe, nor your ears to listen. Abandoning the functions of the eyes and ears, you will finally recognize them.
The Bodhisattva of Sovereignty said: "To look at it and not see it; to listen to it and not hear it; to be free from all extremes—this is called the Wondrous Way.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "If one sees me by form, or seeks me by sound, this person walks a deviant path and cannot perceive the Tathāgata.
The Confucians say: "To see without using the eyes, and to hear without using the ears; to remove the ears..."
The function of the eye naturally attains its true nature. One who is thus will finally know that this True Immortal Bodhisattva is never absent from any place;
sitting together and walking together, sharing joy and laughter, not a single step has ever been taken apart from one another—it is simply that you yourself have remained in ignorance.
Do you wish to see this Bodhisattva? Although he enters and exits without leaving a trace, he shines brilliantly.
Is the radiance visible?
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva constantly manifests wondrous functions and brings forth supernormal powers.
Never departing from his side,
day and night with earnest devotion,
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
Manifesting his body everywhere;
practicing Chan meditation;
reciting the names of the Buddhas and chanting the sutras.
Not fearing birth and death;
craving profit and seeking fame—
everyone possesses these.
Leaving one's father to seek kin;
Avalokiteśvara; the Bodhisattva who brings life; difficult to depict, difficult to paint;
neither form nor emptiness.
Unobstructed and unimpeded,
with an indestructible golden body—
Avalokiteśvara, the living Bodhisattva, who manifests in a thousand transformations.
Simply turn the light back; if you are willing to reflect inwardly, each and every one will achieve perfect realization.
This single word—“cultivation” (*xiū*)—is the path of practice. The way is rugged and steep; without cultivation, it is difficult to traverse.

Now, "cultivation" means cultivating the mind toward the Way, and "practice" (*xíng*) means practicing goodness to return to the Truth. It is like a person repairing a road, clearing away the thorns and brambles that obstruct the way.
When there are stubborn rocks on a path, those that are high are cut away and those that are low are filled in; once swept clean, the way becomes level and smooth.
One’s own mind-ground must likewise be cultivated with such effort: one must eliminate all thoughts of harming others for one's own benefit.
It is like clearing away thorns from a path; one can then ascend the road with steady steps. It is like removing the stubborn rocks obstructing the way;
one is thus able to advance. One should eliminate all distracting thoughts that act as causes and conditions for hindering the Path, purifying the defiled mind and severing all contamination.
To settle and purify [the mind] is the expedient means for entering the gateway of practice at its very beginning. It does not consist in mere verbal discourse, nor does it depend on physical action;
it relies entirely upon applying effort within the ground of the mind. The Immortals and Sages said: "Applying effort within the ground of the mind requires casting aside all worldly affairs.
The Buddhists say: "The Dharma-gate of the ground of the mind does not reside in eloquence of the tongue. The Confucians say: "Speaking is not as good as practicing; practicing is not as good as..."
Upon arriving, one must further examine from where this step arises. If you know the place of its arising, you will know the root source.
Formerly, Liu Haoyue visited Master Baiyun and, after prostrating, asked: "Disciple, my discursive thoughts cannot be subdued;
what should I do? The Master asked: "Who is it that has these discursive thoughts? He replied: "It is I, your disciple. The Master asked again: "And who is it that attempts to subdue them?"
He prostrated himself. Haichue seemed to understand, yet not quite; he remained silent for a moment and then smiled.
The Master said, "Coming and going are entirely up to you, yet you lack mastery. If you cannot overcome him, you must let go. But you must further know who it is that lets go.
If you recognize this, you will possess your own mastery and will no longer be deceived by him. Haichue then attained realization and paid his respects.
It is simply a matter of gratitude. Furthermore, when Master Shishuang asked Master Shitou, "When a thought arises and does not cease, what is it like?

Shitou replied, "Who is it that gives rise to the thought? At this, Shishuang attained great enlightenment. One should simply investigate in this manner, remaining inseparable from it moment after moment.
Wherever the mind and its deliberations arise, one should minutely and carefully examine speech, cognition, and awareness—from where do they emerge?
And he emerged. An ancient said: "If you wish to know where the Buddha has gone, it is simply this speech. Daowu said:

"If you wish to know the fundamental source of the original nature, it does not depart from speech, movement, and stillness. Master Baoyun said: "Listen to one word from me, you who have not yet attained realization:
who is it right now that moves their mouth? Although it is explained in this way, there is an even more wondrous state beyond this—neither cultivated nor...
Practice cannot reach the destination by itself. If one reaches home, then the inquiry into the journey ceases. Furthermore, as for the distance to home:
if one is deluded, it is separated by thousands of mountains and ten thousand rivers; if one awakens, turning one's head is immediately home. Do you understand this principle?
The mind of one who practices goodness is broad; Free from vexation and affliction, they are at peace day and night.
Though the affairs of others are chaotic and tumultuous, Where fame and profit end, joy is spontaneous.
The mind of one who does good is virtuous; Looking ahead and behind, their intentions are ever constant.
Meeting dwellings everywhere, one follows conditions as they arise; In every place, one knows contentment and dwells in peace.
The person who practices the Right Way is like level water; With not an inch of the mind obscured, the myriad dharmas are clear.
Break through the mechanisms of the world and idle affairs will diminish; Having penetrated non-action, the true meets the true.
The person who practices the Way aligns with principle; Thoroughly mastering the Three Teachings, they take refuge entirely in the Way.
This Way is the body of infinite true emptiness; Its principle is the great function within the Way.
The person who practices the Way is profoundly open-hearted; Suddenly, through awakening, they behold the Tathāgata.
The True Buddha constantly manifests without form or appearance; it is a pity that those lacking wisdom cause themselves such deep entanglement through their own [actions].

These three characters—“One,” “Word,” and “Profound”—are subtle, mysterious, and wondrous; they are the place where one penetrates to the very bone and marrow. If you wish to reach this state, [you must practice].
One must indeed clear away [all burdens] until one is light and agile. The Daoist says: "Diminish it again and diminish it again, until one reaches non-action (*wuwei*).

The Buddhist explains: "Put it down, and put it down again; naturally, body and mind will become light and agile. The Confucian says: "If one renews oneself today, one renews oneself day after day, renewing oneself yet again day after day.
To achieve this, one must practice sitting in stillness, clearing away [distractions] day and night, until there is nothing left to sweep away.
It may be swept clean; not even a thread of attachment remains, as if one had been cremated before one’s parents were even born.

As the ancients said: "The undershirt clinging to the body is stripped away. Seeking it within oneself, all is vast and empty; one naturally arrives home. But tell me: why is it that some cannot return home?
The day grows late and the journey is long; the body is weary and the burden is heavy. Having wandered through a hundred thousand lands, one finally returns.
From beginningless time until now,
regarding this most profound place and its mysterious, wondrous principle, no one has attained full understanding;
it is difficult to put into words, and none dare to accept or respond to it.
This is the unconditioned; difficult to measure and difficult to fathom;
ineffable; it is true emptiness;
difficult for people to awaken to; most profoundly subtle and wondrous.
Truly difficult to penetrate; how many know the cause?
Difficult to apply the hand; fundamentally there is not a single thing.
In this most profound place, one sinks without bottom; a single step is difficult to take.
This dharma that is difficult to believe cannot be easily understood;
yet once one attains its profound depths, one rejoices day and night,
with feet firmly planted upon the ground of reality.
Establishing one's destiny and settling the self,
never again to undergo transmigration;
this is the家风 (family style) of formlessness.
Ever-arising and imperishable;
the indestructible golden body;
the boundless realm of the sages.
Enjoyment is inexhaustible;
yet the Illuminating Master failed to explain it thoroughly.
The most profound place is originally my own pure essence—a single segment of numinous clarity.
The two characters "Bānrě" (Prajñā) are Sanskrit terms from the Western Heavens; in the Eastern Land, they are translated as "wisdom.

Generally speaking, one who acts for others must first generate wisdom within themselves. If one lacks wisdom, they are truly a fool, passing their entire life in vain and meekly submitting to the gateway of death.
There is a class of people lacking wisdom who mistake mere cleverness for wisdom; this is a great error. Furthermore, as for cleverness...

The so-called "enlightened person" peddles their vital essence and exhausts their spirit; they employ their mind and heart like a soaring dragon or a swift hawk, yet their actual conduct is like that of a lame tortoise or a humpbacked turtle.
Greedy for profit and seeking fame, they twist the coarse into the refined, regarding worldly wealth as mere bone and marrow.

They cast aside their very lives as if they were mere refuse or soil; concerned only with tomorrow and the day after, this year and the year after, they do not realize that old age is approaching and the limit of death is at hand.
It is a pity that time is wasted in vain and a whole lifetime is spent in such empty toil.
How can one escape the cycle of birth and death? Furthermore, there are those who possess wisdom yet appear foolish and dull in outward conduct, while inwardly...
Be silent and composed. Consciousness undergoes birth and death; realize that there is neither gain nor loss. Constantly observe with clarity: from where does birth come? To where does death go?
Give rise to this single thought, draw near to wise teachers, and consult the perfected ones.

Seek the Dharma that transcends the world and escape the path of birth and death. Avoid transgressions and evils as you would avoid needles and knives; cherish your life and nature as you would cherish your own eyes.

"Beloved one: when active, you bring peace to others and benefit all beings, yet remain undeceived by external conditions. When still, you enter meditative concentration and contemplate emptiness, no longer lingering in the state of wild wandering.
For one who acts thus, once the fruit is perfected, they will wave their hands and return home, attaining great sovereignty."
The former master said: "One day one shall return to one's hometown; no longer a wandering guest. The Commentary says: "Reaching home with hands cast loose, people do not recognize him;
he has nothing further to offer his honored parents. Master Chu'an said: "A solitary boat reaches the shore; a distant traveler returns home."
Tell me, what is this "home"? Far away, it is ten thousand eight thousand miles; near at hand, it does not leave its current place. Do you understand?
Wisdom and intelligence are all the mind itself. The wise cultivate within; the ignorant seek abroad.
If a person possesses wisdom that transcends the three realms, they are free from the ignorance of fools facing birth and death.
With the powerful sword of prajñā-wisdom, they sever craving and thought, escaping the dust and toil of saṃsāra.
They turn their backs on the great limit of the difficult-to-reach and are not spared by the impermanent ghost of death.
Guarding the truth and fulfilling one's resolve is the guiding principle; through rigorous fasting and purification, one naturally attains a noble countenance.
With an iron-like face hanging before him, he does not follow the whims of worldly sentiment, and thus his karmic offenses are extinguished.
The mind of one possessed of wisdom does not wander; though his outward conduct may appear dull and simple, his inner state is tranquil and composed.
Moment by moment remain in the Way without letting it go; From time to time apply your mind and silently practice.
When the work is accomplished and conduct perfected, the conditions will arrive:
With a single shout of "Hūṃ," the Way manifests before you— Transversely pervading the ten directions without obstruction, Vertically exhausting the three periods of time with vast application.
The two characters "Bōluó" (Pāra) are Sanskrit terms from the Western Heavens; in this Eastern Land, they are translated as "the Other Shore.

Furthermore, those who are deluded undergo birth and death and fall into the cycle of saṃsāra, remaining only on this shore. Those who awaken transcend birth and death and escape the cycle of saṃsāra, reaching the other shore.
To reach the other shore, one must personally generate wisdom to cross this sea of suffering of birth and death, just as a person...

Crossing water: when the water is deep and difficult to cross, one must employ boats, bridges, wooden planks, or bamboo rafts—using various skillful means to carry oneself across this sea of suffering to reach the other shore.
Once the other shore has been reached, the aforementioned boats, bridges, wooden planks, and such items are entirely useless.
It is the same for those who perceive their nature and awaken to the Way. As Dadian said: "It is like a blind person..."
Suppose a person seeks a physician. Because the road is far, he cannot travel by himself and must rely on someone to lead him; furthermore, he must have a staff in his hand for it to be possible.
Without these two things, he cannot reach his destination. Once he arrives at the physician’s house, the physician applies ointment to his eyes, and he sees great radiance.
At that point, both the staff and the person leading him are of no further use. Awakening suddenly to the true path of Nirvana is also just like this.
It is so. Now tell me, what is it that drags people along with the staff? I shall now explain it for you; those who believe should simply act.
Thereafter, you must cultivate inner realization and seek the method for seeing one's nature to resolve the great matter of birth and death.

When this practice is perfected in a single day and you behold your original face, that itself is the staff. Furthermore, you must go to visit enlightened masters and true great virtuous ones. Then...
"This is a physician. From the many expedient means employed previously, none have been effective; only this staff must not be discarded. The Daoists say:

"When one has caught the fish, one forgets the trap; when one has caught the rabbit, one forgets the snare. The Buddhists say: "To cross the river, one must use a raft; once the shore is reached, the boat is no longer needed. The Confucians say:

"When one has grasped the meaning, one forgets the words; when one has obtained the rice, one forgets the field. Since the Daoists, Buddhists, and Confucians all teach that one must forget, for what reason?
I simply do not teach you to discard this staff. Seek until you reach the end of waters and the limits of mountains;
let it remain as a companion to pass the time. Have you even considered this? This staff has no inherent characteristics from the start; fundamentally, it is no different from empty space.
If a person can lift it up and penetrate through the three heavens, the demons throughout the world will not dare to look upon them. *Prajñā*—
one who has reached the shore, who treads the solid earth and practices goodness,
shall emerge from the sea of suffering and no longer be submerged in the dust of the world.
To penetrate the Great Way and clarify the principles of nature— there is yet a way to return home.
Reaching one's own ground, establishing destiny and settling the self:
the Buddhas of the three periods are all here, within the oceanic assembly of the Avataṃsaka.
In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, one enjoys the splendor of its scenery;
Yet from within the sea of suffering, where waves toss and boiling waters run deep, Thoughts arise endlessly and without limit;
With no boat to ferry one across, there is no way to escape with life.
Day and night at home, fearing birth and death, with endless sorrow he sought an enlightened master;
not finding one, how could he escape the crimson tide?
Then he saw a man who spoke of the Buddha-dharma, and at that sound he cried out aloud.
Discoursing on the unconditioned, expounding upon principles and meanings:
the original nature is fundamentally such that every word is true and every phrase is correct. Alone, one is a companion to oneself;
the three teachings are the same. This accords with the holy mind and is dispassionate toward the world.
This principle is that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
The Samādhi of Universal Radiance sweeps away the myriad dharmas, Splitting open the gate of mystery.
With the heart’s joy piercing through heaven and earth, It can be trusted and accepted— There is not another single thought.
*Bōluómì* (Pāramitā): "Climbing to the Other Shore.
These two characters, *mìduō* (mitra), are the Sanskrit language of the Western Heaven; in the Eastern Land, they are translated as "The Infinite" (*wújí*).

Now, as for "the infinite," it is the infinite that is the Great Ultimate (*tài jí*). It is the wondrous Way of empty space. As the ancients said: "The infinite gives rise to the Great Ultimate. The Great...
The ultimate divides into the two polarities. The two polarities give rise to the three powers. The three powers give rise to the four images. The four images give rise to the five elements.
Because the five elements exist, all things gradually proliferate. All these myriad categories are fully encompassed within the wondrous Dao.

Now, the single character "honey" (蜜) serves as a metaphor for the wondrous Way of empty space. The term "many" (多) is compared to the various categories and types of beings, both sentient and insentient, all of which are encompassed within the Way.
For instance, it is like a bee gathering from a hundred flowers to ferment and produce honey.
Before it has been completed, there are the various flavors of salty, sour, sweet, bitter, and pungent, and the various colors of blue, yellow, red, and white;

these flavors are unequal and these colors are not uniform. Once the work is finished and the honey is produced, all those various flavors are fermented into a single flavor, and all those diverse colors blend into a single color.
As for its fragrant and delicious taste, there is no distinction whatsoever. Upon reaching this state—
Thus, the bees obtain sustenance and people obtain utility. It is the same for those who practice the Way.

For instance, when a practitioner disciplines the body and mind, grinding them in the morning and refining them in the evening, before their meritorious practice has reached completion, there may still arise a mind of stinginess and greed, a mind of profit and fame, a mind of jealousy, a mind of cruelty, a mind of calculation, a mind of victory and defeat, a mind of arrogance, and a mind of "self."
A mind of pride; a mind of murderous intent; a mind of the three poisons; a mind of fear and dread; a mind of deceit and concealment; a mind of false conceptualization;
a mind of ignorance; a mind of delusion and turbidity; a mind of unwholesomeness; a mind that deceives others; a nature of violence and evil; a nature of coarseness and agitation;

a nature of wind and fire; a nature of dogmatic views; a nature of contrariness and inferiority; a nature of emptiness and falsehood; a nature fond of quarreling; a nature of stubbornness and forcefulness; a nature of instability and deception; a nature of superficiality and vanity; a nature of flattery.
The nature of crookedness; the nature of discrimination; the nature of greed and anger; the nature of affectionate attachment; the nature of fickleness.
Since beginningless time, all these habitual tendencies and greedy minds exceed eighty-four thousand; they cannot be fully described. This is for those of wisdom.
Cutting through with a single stroke, one resolves to protect oneself. By exhausting the root and investigating the source, merit becomes perfected and practice fulfilled.

The stubborn mind naturally ceases and perverse natures are extinguished. The sacred mind and true nature are revealed, without any distinction; the true and eternal alone is manifest, attaining great sovereignty. As an ancient worthy said:
"The myriad stars may shine brightly, yet they do not equal the solitary moon shining alone. Master Dao said: "The hundred rivers flow..."
There is exhaustion; yet a single ocean contains the infinite. The Immortal Master said: "A thousand thoughts and ten thousand anxieties ultimately result in delusion;
guard only the one truth, and the Way will naturally draw near. But tell me, how does one come to see that one truth?
The two protections of Prajñāpāramitā are no ordinary matters; All things are refined and returned to their original source.
When used, its sweetness lingers within the heart; Though various flavors differ, they are all uniformly sweet.
Through compassion and skillful means, all people rejoice; It is gentle, kind, and benevolent, honored with respect and tolerance.
Realizing that the fundamental nature is empty and functions according to conditions, one may step forward to shoulder the responsibility at the moment of life’s end;
with a heart of faith, receive the boundless Way. When the Great Function is unimpaired, the principle and meaning are complete;
with an iron face devoid of sentimentality, birth and death are severed. Let go of doubt, and you will find peace in that very instant.
It is not urgent to realize impermanence, But it is most difficult to give rise to wisdom.
To follow the six thieves is to invite disaster; The mind-monkey and will-horse are most unruly.
When sin arises for one person, it is hard to escape suffering; Do not sink into the abyss, but exert yourself in contemplation.
Regretting that my ritual deportment could not be further refined, I lightly leapt out of the coffin of right and wrong.
At that moment, for one living in this world, there are many who lack clarity; yet at once awakening, the ground of the mind becomes transparently clear.
One recognizes that myriad conditions are false and understands that worldly affairs are but empty flowers. Turning the light back upon itself directly, one then—
One attains purity. This purity spontaneously accords with the Way. An ancient worthy said: "The clear breeze rustles, penetrating the heart;
at this moment, its joy is difficult for people to recognize. It is more profound than the profound, more wondrous than the wondrous. There is no east, west, south, or north;
there are no four intermediate directions, nor above or below. There is no past, future, or present. It is equal to empty space and non-different from the Great Way.
2. They both return at the same time, and there are not two separate places. Master Chuanshou said: "At every moment, the clear wind and bright moon are ever-present companions.
When asked about the red peach and white plum, or the purple rose, the Lord of the East knows nothing at all. Tell me, where does the Lord of the East take his stand?
Do you see him? He cannot be struck away; he cannot be cut to death. He is in the red peach and the white plum; he is in the rose.
Violet. Hehe. For a moment, reflections arose:
In this world of human life, one seeks food and clothing;
Day and night one is busy, unable to find rest.
With a mind of deluded thoughts, one seeks wealth and status; competing for fame and seizing profit, they display their stubbornness.
They can twist and manipulate others, exhausting their spirit without yielding.
With a heart darkened by blood-money, they deceive Heaven and transgress the Way.
One by one, they cast aside their lives, Disregarding this wretched remainder of their present existence.
Having attained this human body, It is not at all easy;
now they face the limit of punishment. These ghosts of those who died unjustly Shall never again turn over.
The eyes are not blind, and the ears are not deaf; Having seen this model, cease from imitating others.
You dull-witted people, do not let your time pass in vain waiting for it;
When the great limit arrives, it will be like digging a well when thirsty.
At that time, impermanence arrives; how can one find a way to stop it?
Seize this present moment while the four elements are at peace. With a steadfast mind, advance further so that the body remains free of illness;
do not be complacent in your health, but prepare for the journey ahead.
The luminous mind, the nature of seeing— Transcending the ordinary and surpassing the holy, it is naturally attained. The bright pearl is revealed;
Its essence is transparent, exquisite, and bare. A single radiance Is placed before one’s eyes.
Vividly clear, no longer hidden; The golden body constantly manifests, day and night.
Radiating light, unimpeded in every direction— Upon reaching such a state, One’s own future destiny is assured.
To be a seeker of the Way, one must resolve to cultivate the spirit;
thus, emerging from the sea of suffering, one reaches the peace and nourishment of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Therein, one establishes oneself in excellence and perceives that the five aggregates are all empty. It is said that the four elements are not substantial. As for the five aggregates: they are form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Furthermore, because these five aggregates accumulate without dispersing, one falsely identifies the physical body as the self; thus, one wanders in saṃsāra for long kalpas.

If a person awakens with fierce resolve and, using this illusory body, practices according to the teachings, they will constantly reflect inwardly until they perceive the five aggregates to be utterly pure and exhausted.
Now tell me: what are form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness? How can these five aggregates all be made empty?
I shall now speak plainly and clearly. If there are those who understand these words, let them cease their doubts and, with faith and acceptance, put them into practice;

then there will surely come a day when you accord with the Way. Furthermore, as for "form" (rūpa), it carries the meaning of obstruction. If, upon encountering circumstances or meeting objects, one does not cling to them nor become defiled by them, then there is no obstruction;
the aggregate of form is itself empty. As for "feeling" (vedanā), it carries the meaning of reception. If one encounters...

Regarding all objects of sound and form, the mind does not grasp them; thus one attains the emptiness of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). "Perception" (*saṃjñā*) refers to the meaning of deluded thoughts and deliberations.
If one does not reflect on the past, has no perceptions regarding the future, and remains as it is in the present, one attains the emptiness of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

"Volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*) refers to the meaning of the ceaseless movement and flux of mental activity. If, throughout the twelve periods of the day, the mind does not wander outward, [one attains the emptiness of the aggregate of volitional formations].

Mindfulness is neither distracted nor confused; it is not turned by external things, nor detained by sensory objects. A single thought does not depart from its proper place, and thus one attains the emptiness of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
As for "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), it refers to the principle of discriminating between the near and the distant, as well as the principle of clinging to objects.

If, when seeing all objects and things, one makes no distinctions or identifications whatsoever, but regards them all with uniform equanimity—seeing yet as if not seeing, cognizing yet as if not cognizing—[then consciousness is empty].
Consciousness has no kinship and no distance; when it comes, respond to it; when it goes, do not think of it. Thus one attains the emptiness of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Once this stage is reached, one naturally perceives that all five aggregates are empty. The six sense-apertures are bright and pure—purely naked, starkly bare, with nothing to grasp.
Furthermore, even the names "four elements" and "five aggregates" cannot be found. As it is said: [The Way].
"Only emptiness is seen. The commentary states: "Empty space is revealed alone. Formerly, when King Kali was out hunting, he encountered an immortal (ṛṣi).
When the king questioned him, the immortal did not answer. The king first sliced off his left shoulder, then his right arm, and finally dismembered him limb by limb;
yet the immortal’s face showed no fear, nor did his expression change at all. Furthermore, the King of Kaśmīra asked the Venerable Siṃha: "What are you doing here?"
"What is it? the Venerable replied. "It is that these aggregates (*skandhas*) are empty. The King asked, "Have you attained the emptiness of the aggregates?
The Venerable said, "I have already attained the dharma of the emptiness of the aggregates. The King said, "Can I obtain your head, Master? The Venerable said, "My body is not mine;
how much less so my head? Furthermore, Dharma Master Zhao said: "The four great elements are fundamentally without self; the five aggregates are all entirely empty. Taking his head...
A white blade is like cutting the spring breeze. Furthermore, when Śāriputra saw the goddess, he asked her, "Why do you not transform out of this female body?
The goddess replied, "For twelve years I have sought my female body, yet it is utterly unfindable.
What, then, am I to transform? Again, when Master Jingqing had been at his monastery for three years, the local guardian deity of the temple wished to see him.
Yan could not do it. Furthermore, the Real Man Hao of Taigu was practicing the Way beneath the bridge in Zhaozhou.
One night, he suddenly heard a multitude of ghosts conversing by the riverbank, saying: "Tomorrow, a man wearing an iron cap will come to replace us."
Having finished speaking, there was no further sign or sound. When the next day arrived, as dusk fell, a heavy rain suddenly began.

[Tao Gu] saw a man walking across the bridge, shielding himself from the rain with an iron cauldron balanced upon his head; he had washed his feet under the bridge before crossing. Upon seeing him, Tao Gu shouted, "Do not wash!
Hearing the words of the True Man (Zhenren), the man supported himself on the railing and continued across the bridge. That night, all the ghosts arrived. One ghost...
He said, "For three years or more, we had obtained a single substitute, but this master has ruined it.
The various ghosts, wishing to harm the True Man, came and went searching for him but could not find him; they did not know where the True Man was and departed with sighs of lamentation.
The True Man remained right beneath the bridge, yet the ghosts were unable to see him. Furthermore, when Master Hongjue resided in his hermitage, the Celestial Kitchen sent [him provisions].
After making offerings, he went to visit Master Dongshan and then returned to his hermitage. For three days, celestial beings brought offerings but could not find the abbot;

the abbot remained right within the hermitage, yet they could not see him. Why was this? These superior men have all attained the Dharma of sudden and perfect enlightenment and possess the secret method of invisibility;
neither gods nor ghosts can perceive them. The four elements are insubstantial, and this physical body is not permanent.
The five aggregates are entirely empty; this is one's original face. From where was this statement derived?
Who is it that clearly perceives the emptiness of the five aggregates?
The immortal attained the emptiness of the five aggregates; When the King questioned him three times, he did not respond.
The King grew indignant as his corpse decayed, Yet it revealed the indestructible vajra-body.
Venerable Siṃha attained the emptiness of the aggregates; When the King questioned him, he said, "I have no body."
The king does not distinguish between those who are beheaded; though they die, they have no fear as their nature returns to emptiness.
The Dharma Master understands that the five aggregates are empty; he proclaims the four lines with great clarity.
If there is one who can realize the unconditioned dharma, the blade cannot cleave their original truth.
The Celestial Woman attained the clarity that the five aggregates are empty;
Śāriputra stepped forward, causing the wind of the mechanism to turn the woman into a man, who became an Arhat. Returning delusion to the truth, one is not liberated from birth;
Master Jingqing understood the emptiness of the aggregates— For three years, the local deities saw no trace of him.
The Buddha attained the great supernatural power of benefit; Having realized the Great Way, he feared neither ghosts nor spirits.
Hongjue attained the emptiness of the five aggregates; When gods and humans presented offerings, his traces were nowhere to be seen.
The samādhi of non-action is difficult to fathom; The secret of invisibility reveals its wondrous efficacy.
Recognizing this and turning back, one immediately applies effort; with clear detachment, one awakens to the emptiness of the mind.
Let worldly affairs fall away as they may; within them lies another, extraordinary power.

As for those who cross over all suffering and calamity: the Buddha, out of compassion for sentient beings, revealed the provisional to manifest the ultimate, transcending birth and death so that they may attain liberation.
The suffering of saṃsāra. The Most High said: "I have a great affliction: that I have a body. If I had no body, what affliction would I have?
The Śramaṇa says: "The body is the root of all sufferings. The Confucian says: "With a body there is affliction; without grasping there is no sorrow."
The Sūtra says: "The three realms offer no peace; they are like a burning house, filled with manifold sufferings and most terrifying.
If there is a person of wisdom who reflects back upon themselves, they realize that their own body is entirely illusory and not real—how much more so other things?
In a single day, impermanence will cause everything to be cast away, rendering it useless in a hundred ways. If one contemplates this moment by moment, the mind..."

Objects will naturally vanish and discursive thoughts will naturally diminish. Furthermore, you must visit and consult with spiritual friends and draw near to the wise, seeking the path to liberation and resolving the great matter of birth and death.
Suddenly, one day, with a single "crash" on the ground, you will cast off the bottom of the lacquer bucket and see your original face.
Do you wish to see your original face? It has never changed throughout the past or present; it is only that people themselves fail to recognize it.
True. The enlightened master has explained it thoroughly:
originally, this very mind—once the mind is realized as empty, suffering simply ceases to exist. What birth and death could there be? What things could there be?
One day, having cast off the coarse garment of the mortal womb, one becomes a carefree Great Man.
With firm resolve training in the Way like the Tathāgata, Delivering all beings from suffering, distress, and calamity;
Constantly observing the fast until the end like the Tathāgata,
Not begrudging body or life like the Tathāgata.
Compassion and skillful means resemble the Tathāgata;
filial piety toward one's parents resembles the Tathāgata;
the vastness of the gates of practice resembles the Tathāgata.
Discerning neither poverty nor wealth is like the Tathāgata;
Taming and guiding men is like the Tathāgata;
Teaching others to settle the mind is like the Tathāgata.
The manifestation of the attainment of the Way resembles that of a Tathāgata.
"Śāriputra" distinguishes between the two modalities of the provisional and the real. "Śā" (舍) means a house; this refers to the physical body composed of the four great elements.
"Lizǐ" (利子) refers to the originally inherent, singular, numinous true nature within that house—the master who wields the staff of the firm and solid essence. It is like...
The guest-house owner stays for a short time. If the owner leaves the house, the building immediately collapses. Interest and profit remain constant;
it is merely that one changes houses to dwell in. The Master said: "The body is the dwelling of the vital breath (*qi*); the mind is the abode of the spirit (*shen*).

After a long time, the spirit and breath disperse, which is another form of moving house. The Commentary says: Since beginningless time, we have been renting houses to live in; until now, who has ever [owned them]?
"Recognize the master of consciousness. Yaoshan further said: "When skin and flesh have fallen away entirely, there remains only the one true reality.
Do you wish to see this true reality? Do you yet recognize this [circle]? He also said: "Coming and going for thousands of times."
It is simply that the people of the world cannot grasp it.
A single hut of four great thatched huts, Containing heaven, earth, and the mountains and rivers;
within it dwells a true immortal, Untainted by even a speck of dust—the Great Mahā (Abiding in the Great Lavana).
Śāriputra has always lived together with me; The physical body has form, but its nature is unconditioned.
This nature is true emptiness and cannot be destroyed; That which has form is inevitably driven toward death.
Śāriputra was originally a steadfast son; This physical body will soon turn into a mound of ash.
Faithfully accept that your own true *śarīra* has never been separated from you since beginningless time;
this *śarīra* is your original master. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, it is always present within the body.
Though it manifests in a thousand transformations and ten thousand uses as the vessel of the body, its essence is fundamentally seen to be empty.
That "form is not different from emptiness" means there is no further discrimination. The nature of the Way is non-dual; true emptiness is uniform and equal, ever-present before one's eyes.

It manifests forms in response to things, yet people all fail to recognize it. For the long, it is the emptiness of the long; for the short, the emptiness of the short; for the square, the emptiness of the square;
for the round, the emptiness of the round; for the white, the emptiness of the white; for the red, the emptiness of the red; for the small, the emptiness of the small; for the large—

The Great Emptiness. That which is distant is empty as the distant; that which is near is empty as the near. The Way says: "It is inherently possessed by every person; there is none who lacks it. The Commentary says:
"All wriggling creatures and sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. The Confucians say: "All sentient beings each possess a single Great Ultimate (*tài jí*).
An ancient worthy further said: "In every atom is the Way; in every atom is the Buddha. The Immortals and Perfected Ones say: "What thing does not receive [this nature]?"
The Way arises. What thing does not receive the transformation of the Way? It manifests forms according to its location and acts with mastery wherever it is.

The Way is not distant from people; it is people who distance themselves from it. When one turns back to observe one’s own body as form, within that form there must be the true emptiness of awakened nature (*bodhicitta*).

It responds by manifesting all manner of appearances; these various appearances are precisely what is manifested by the true emptiness of awakened nature. Yongjia said: "Illusory transformations are empty..."

The body is itself the Dharma-body. The Dharma-body is fully awakened to the fact that there is not a single thing; it is the original source-nature, the true and natural Buddha. The Immortal Master said:
"The physical form is a provisional appearance, yet within it is contained the true form which is signless. Master Baoming said: "Within the body with signs is the signless body;
this signless body radiates light throughout the day. Do you understand this?
Form is not different from emptiness; their essence is merged. The Tathāgatas of the three periods cultivate the *milare* (union);
the myriad dharmas return to the single essence of *dhyāna*. Ordinary beings and sages dwell together in the essence of *dhyāna*;
the Great Way is undivided, its meaning level and impartial. The eighth is the realization of the unconditioned, clarifying liberation.
Obstructed and unable to find a place of peace, they are foremost in contention and exhaust themselves.
Having committed evil deeds in past lives, they transmigrate through saṃsāra; though born as humans in this life, they remain entirely ignorant.
Upon hearing or encountering what is wholesome, they harbor resentment in their hearts; because the roots of their karma are deep and heavy, they wander further from liberation.
Having cultivated cause and effect since beginningless time, And having planted the great foundation over many kalpas, One encounters auspicious matters with joy;
Concentration, rectitude, and perfect luminosity are equal to the Buddha’s.
That emptiness is no different from form—though the branches differ slightly, the root is without distinction. Form and emptiness are originally of one kind. Worldly people...

Regarding "Self-discrimination": The Daoist says: "The Great Square has no corners; it is a unified, indistinguishable whole. The Buddhist says: "The three thousandfold world-system is consolidated into a single world.
The Confucian says: "Ascending Mount Dong, one makes Lu seem small; ascending Mount Tai, one makes the world seem small.
When the barriers are removed, what is 'that' and what is 'this'? The Ancients say: "Worthy sages constantly practice the wisdom of equality, giving rise to no marks of discrimination."
The sages and saints of the Three Teachings are also empty; the four modes of birth and the six paths of existence are also empty.
From the immortals and Buddhas above down to the crawling insects, grasses, and trees below, every single one is fundamentally empty.

Furthermore, before the Great Simplicity had dispersed, before Yin and Yang had been distinguished, before the Two Polarities had been divided, and before the Three Powers had been established—what "you" and "I" could there have been? Fundamentally, all were but a single principle. Because...

The Great Simplicity disperses; heaven and earth unite. The Three Powers are established, and the myriad beings multiply and flourish. Why is it that, even until now, they cannot return to the source?
It is simply because sentient beings cling to attachments; they do not know that all is originally empty. They delude themselves and pursue external objects.
The mind gives rise to inverted views and follows the flow of phenomena, unable to return to oneness. Because capacities and insights differ, one becomes attached to form or to emptiness;
these are the two views of form and emptiness. If a person here realizes the voidness of emptiness with total clarity, such that there is nothing remaining within or without body and mind—
One does not perceive emptiness as form; one is not driven by things, nor deceived by circumstances. All is uniformly equal—how could there be duality? Thus, one attains the return to the One.
Yet even this "One" is already an excess. The Patriarch Chongyang said: "Embracing the Origin and guarding the One is the practice;
when earth and heaven endure for eternity, even the One is gone. An ancient said: "The myriad dharmas return to the One; to what does the One return? The One.
The essential point of the place of return you must know. Tell me, where does one return? A dog licking a hot oil cauldron.
Emptiness is not different from form; this manifests the prior cause. At the very beginning, there was originally no division;
before any judgment was made, there was not a single thing. Above and below, the profound void is a single expanse of emptiness.
Without yin and without yang, without heaven and earth, How could there be sun and moon along with the stars?
Without male and without female, without sages or worthies, And without the three teachings—there was no trace at all.
From the red and the dark, the sprouts divided into the Three Rituals; In the dimming of fortune, the primal qi first arose.
From Pangu until today, one follows along with the myriad things;

Man dwells within them, yet follows the five elements and turns his back on the light to cast himself into darkness, his mind failing to penetrate through. He does not contemplate returning to the source to seek the firm root;
This body is the convergence of the parents' yin and yang— Where, then, can one find the Buddha-nature through such schemes and deliberations?
"Form is itself emptiness" distinguishes the principles of the heterodox and the orthodox. Emptiness resides within form, yet it is difficult for worldly people to perceive. The eye is form;
it cannot see objects by itself—it is only the wondrous capacity of true emptiness that can see. The ear is form;
it cannot hear sounds by itself—it is only the wondrous capacity of true emptiness that can hear sounds. The nose is form; it cannot discern fragrances or stenches by itself—only...
This wondrous nature of true emptiness is able to perceive fragrance and stench. The tongue is form; it cannot speak. It is only this wondrous nature of true emptiness that can speak.
The body is form; it cannot perceive touch. It is only this wondrous nature of true emptiness that can perceive touch.
The feet are form; they cannot walk. It is only this wondrous nature of true emptiness that can walk. The hands are form.

It cannot be grasped or lifted. Only the wondrous nature of true emptiness can grasp and lift it. Now, as for this wondrous nature of true emptiness: it has no eyes yet can see; it has no ears yet can hear;
it has no nose yet can smell; it has no tongue yet can speak; it has no feet yet can walk; it has no hands yet can grasp.
The faculty of the mind (manas) has a name but no form; it is divided into eighty-four thousand modes of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. In total—
They return to the six sense faculties, where the functions of all parts of the body interpenetrate in wondrous spiritual powers.

As the ancients said: "The whole body is it; every part of the body is it. Master Dao said: "There is no need to search far elsewhere; throughout the twelve periods of the day, it revolves within the entire body.

Form and emptiness are not different, and the wondrous principle is fully manifest. What can be called form is not true form; what can be called emptiness is not true emptiness. All things ultimately return to the Great Way."
This is emptiness. Now tell me, how is this principle? The Old Man Chuan said: "To have form and to have seeking are both delusions;
to be formless and shadowless is to fall into partiality and barrenness. Magnificent and profound, how could there ever be an interval? A single cold light pierces the great void."
The Master said: "To know that emptiness is not empty, and to know that form is not form—this is called 'clear illumination. I cannot help but speak plainly now:

when you encounter any object with marks, do not allow yourself to become stained by attachment. When you reach the state where emotions are forgotten and thoughts are severed, do not allow yourself to lose sight of the Truth.
To cling to marks is to dwell in existence; to lose sight of the Truth is to fall into emptiness. Only when you do not dwell in existence..."
This is one who has realized the truth:
form is itself emptiness, gold within the ore. Buried in the dust for thousands of springs, they have applied their minds to sift through the sand to find the treasure.
The enlightened master points it out, and the golden body appears.
With the eyes one beholds all golden bodies appearing; With the ears one hears all golden bodies appearing;
With the nose one smells all golden bodies appearing; With the mouth one speaks all golden bodies appearing;
With the hands one grasps all golden bodies appearing; With the feet one travels ten thousand li, with all golden bodies appearing.
Realizing the essence, the luminous golden body manifests; The mind’s transformations, when examined in detail, reveal the thousandfold and myriad changes of the golden body manifesting;
Day and night, as it patrols, the golden body manifests;
In its swift movements and grasping of grass, the golden body manifests; Having realized this great function, no trace is seen.
The Great Way is not apart from the square inch of the heart; there is no need to search for it far away in other places.
That "emptiness is itself form" has been explained in detail again and again. Form exists within emptiness; otherwise, people would be deceived by external objects. The Immortal Master said:
"If the Way did not possess the myriad phenomena, it could not manifest; if the myriad phenomena did not possess the Way, they could not arise. The commentary says: "To see..."

When form is seen, emptiness is perceived; when there is no form, emptiness is not seen. Therefore, the sages and worthies of the three teachings do not perceive the existence of form or the existence of emptiness.

Form and emptiness are both extinguished; there is no distinction between internal and external. Suchness is eternally spontaneous, its radiance penetrating and shining throughout all lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Worldly people, however, are not thus; they distinguish between the internal and the external, and argue about "that" and "this," becoming attached to appearances and divisions.

Separate. Seeing various forms, following sounds and chasing colors, one is deluded regarding the truth and remains unaware. From one shell to another, from one existence to the next, one wanders on without knowing it;
changing heads and swapping faces, there is no end in sight. This is not the business of others; it is what you have sought out for yourself.
Why do you not turn back early to save yourself? Tell me, how can you be saved? Cast away the old pitcher of foul water. Select...
Apply the golden needle to the point of pain.
Emptiness is form—neither is real; Form is emptiness—the two are deficient and distinct.
The two extremes and the middle are the path of birth and death; When both form and emptiness are extinguished together, one falls into ease.
All phenomena that possess marks are empty and false;

Having realized the unconditioned, to speak of the conditioned is to kill the Buddhas and destroy the Patriarchs, meeting with punishment from the King of Yama. The ghosts come to pursue those who provoke his wrath;
If you are a latecomer in your studies, you must first attain the Way of Buddhahood, for it is already too late to practice for long.
When can one ever finish studying the myriad dharmas? They deceive the deluded by showing them these gathered collections;
when the great limit arrives, there is no fixed certainty. If the mind-ground is not clear, how can one escape?
If there is someone who understands the patriarch’s pivot, a single phrase will instantly transcend billions of worlds.
All things are uniform and level; what difference could there be? Originally, one is but a single household.
It is only because of clinging to the branches and twigs that one has lost sight of the sprout of the Great Way from before.

As for sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—these are the states of a greedy mind that finds no end. Because of seeing with the eyes, one experiences forms; because of experiencing forms...

The mind possesses ideation; because of ideation, there is mental formation (*saṃskāra*). Because of mental formation, there is cognition (*vijñāna*). There are the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*);
because of the six sense faculties, the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) arise. With the emergence of consciousness, there are the four great elements and the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Possessing this physical body of the five aggregates, one becomes attached to appearances and engages in discrimination, pursuing sounds and chasing forms, giving rise to hatred, love, sorrow, and fear from this point onward, thereby leading to the cycle of wandering births.

Death follows without ceasing. If you wish to sever birth and death and bring an end to saṃsāra, simply illuminate the single root from which they arise and cause the four elements and five aggregates to be completely purified.
Then, all will be vast and empty, devoid of self; immediately, one is tranquil and still.

Directly take responsibility for your own nature prior to the void kalpa—a state that is silent yet ever-illuminating, illuminating yet ever-silent. As the Supreme One said: "Silence has no location..."

In stillness, how could desire arise? Since desire does not arise, this is true tranquility. It is further said: "One perceives only emptiness; one contemplates that emptiness as empty. Emptiness has nothing to be emptied.
Since that which is emptied is non-existent, even 'non-existence' is non-existent. Since both [existence and] non-existence are non-existent, there is profound, eternal stillness.
The commentary explains: "The person is empty and phenomena are empty; these two aspects are fundamentally identical. Furthermore, contemplate the person and phenomena..."
The two emptinesses—where, ultimately, do they abide? All objects and myriad conditions cannot detain them; they are indistinctly hidden within the great void.
Sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness harbor deep attachments and cravings; from time immemorial, they have fallen into the cycle of delusion.
Turning back and forth, the Sahā world revolves; Traces are extinguished as they traverse the four modes of birth:
From womb-birth come camels, mules, and transformed elephants and horses; From egg-birth come birds and beasts, changing into winged fowl;
From moisture-birth come those in the water, transformed into shrimp and crabs; Through transformation-birth, one becomes a mosquito or a gnat within the evil realms.
Falling from the Way, one suffers for immeasurable kalpas; The tears shed upon the bones are as numerous as dust motes.
Those suffering through the four modes of birth are difficult to save; Calling out to their faces, they are reborn within the six realms.
Having once received blessings among humans and devas, They now become sentient beings within the paths of humans and devas.
Within the realm of hell, there is boundless suffering; In the realm of hungry ghosts, one is drenched in molten copper;
In the realm of animals, one wanders through various destinies;
In the realm of asuras, one serves as a celestial soldier— Having transmigrated through all four modes of birth and six realms, Lord Yama, Kṣitigarbha, arouse your compassionate heart!
"Apply yourself to being human and seek the Way; do not again enter the gates of my hell.
Reform evil and cultivate goodness, practicing cause and effect. If you wish to become a venerable one, I shall not be angry;
it is likewise for those who act thus. This is the meaning of returning to the source. Since there is no self, all phenomena are non-existent; they return once more to—
Emptiness. One thereby attains the return to the source and the restoration to the origin. In the Buddha-faith, this is called "the myriad dharmas returning to the One.
In the Daoist tradition, it is called "returning to life and its root. In the Confucian tradition, it is called "returning to the primordial state of the Heavenly Principle.

Reaching this point, the path of words is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases. If one stirs a thought, one deviates; if one makes arrangements, it is not so. Therefore, the Old Man of Chuang [said]:
He said, "Step back, step back! Look, look! Even a stubborn rock makes the earth tremble. Do you understand? Stop this senseless wandering;
if you move, you shall receive thirty blows."
Extremely clear: today one has finally attained the vision of the Tathāgata in this very same way.
When the mind gives rise to the eye, one again attains the fruition, sees the Tathāgata, and knows the underlying principle and meaning.
Returning to the root and preserving the life-force; purity and cleanliness;
attaining manifest realization; true emptiness;
entering the great gate; non-action.
The Ultimate Way: Natural Simplicity.
To settle body and life—this wondrous instruction penetrates the heart in a single word.
That which is called the Śāriputra is one's own original nature. Failing to recognize it face-to-face, it cannot be burned by fire nor drowned by water; even arrows [cannot harm it].
It cannot be wounded; a blade cannot cut it. The wind cannot blow it away; the sun cannot scorch it. The rain cannot drench it;
it cannot be depicted in a painting. Poisonous drugs cannot harm it; malevolent insects cannot sting it. It is all because one has taken the wrong path in one's journey.
This is why they have lost the *pāramitās*. Have you seen Śāriputra? From antiquity until now, he has never changed;
he simply comes and goes, renting houses to dwell in—sometimes in vermilion towers and painted pavilions, sometimes in thatched huts and grass-roofed halls.
Sometimes golden nails on vermilion doors; sometimes broken temples and kiln niches. Do you understand? Old Chuang said:
"Clouds rise over the southern mountains, rain falls on the northern peaks. How many names for horses and how many characters for donkeys?

Look at the vast and boundless waters without emotion—where do they follow the square, and where do they follow the round? If you wish to avoid coming and going, you must attain the exhaustion of outflows and return home.
Quiescent extinction. One such as this forever transcends the three realms; heaven and earth cannot constrain them. They become a carefree person beyond all things.
Do you understand? It is better to retreat than to press forward.
Śāriputra, all that is conditioned is joined with the noble; when joined in one place, the noble is firm and stable.
That which is conditioned is not long-lasting; its forms are not enduring and lack substantiality.
Some are empty and false; those who refuse to investigate them deeply will not realize this.
I have betrayed the intent of the Tathāgata;
Reluctant to investigate and contemplate the Heart Sūtra, Every day I merely wander about counting characters.
If I were to meet a true teacher And exhaustively explore the meaning of principle, My heart would not remain in such turmoil.
Resolve your will and arouse fierce vigor; cease this dull and stubborn study.
Once you have thoroughly penetrated it, O Śāriputra—you who pierce through earth and heaven, the King of Dharmas, who manifests in a thousand transformations—[you shall realize the truth].
Constantly emitting rays from the brow-hair,
indestructible throughout eternal kalpas,
the true void is boundless.
Śāriputra, the King of Dharmas, who neither comes nor goes,
is precisely the Western Land of Ultimate Great Way.
With a mind-ground as firm as stone, one penetrates through; Seeing the śarīra relics before one, one honors the Buddha-Dharma;
Drawing near to teachers, one does not disdain asking questions of those below;
Seeking the true principle and investigating the ultimate meaning, One shall avoid meeting King Yama.
Regarding these "dharmas characterized by emptiness": this refutes the heterodox and reveals the orthodox; all dharmas are empty, and fundamentally they are not the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The Immortal Zhen said: "Dharmas are fundamentally no-dharmas; forms are fundamentally non-forms. Having form is ultimately a fabrication;

being without marks is the True Person. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Even dharmas should be relinquished, let alone non-dharmas. It further states: "All that has marks is entirely void."
Delusion! If one perceives that all marks are non-marks, one then sees the Tathāgata.

As for the ancestral masters of old who spoke of the single flavor of emptiness, it was solely because sentient beings are fundamentally empty, yet they carry this burden without acting upon it; thus, they established various provisional names to guide both the animate and the inanimate toward emptiness and stillness, so that they might return to the original source.
If your faith has not yet reached this point, simply go and sit in quietude to reflect.
Illumination. Illuminatingly seeing that the five aggregates are truly non-existent, one naturally forgets form and forgets substance, thereby attaining the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

Once the emptiness of persons is attained, it is like a medicine being discarded once the illness has been cured; the dharmas are also empty. When both person and dharma are empty, one naturally comes to rest and finds cessation.

As the Sutra says: "My body was originally non-existent; from what source could hatred and love arise? Having thus attained the forgetting of form and the forgetting of substance, [one abides in peace].
There are no profound anxieties that can entangle one once this ground is reached; naturally, everything is set down.

There are no sages or Buddhas to be made, no birth-and-death to be severed, and nothing to cultivate or realize. If there were even a hair’s breadth more to cultivate or realize, one would fall into the realm of birth-and-death and suffer perpetual sinking for kalpas.
If one can thoroughly cast off all attachments and remain without dependence, one does not fall into existence.
There are no two extremes; it stands alone like space. To directly accept this—what is there that is not possible in that which is perfectly round and brilliantly radiant even before the empty kalpa?
Do you understand? Heaven and earth are two lotuses in the sea; all sentient beings emerge and submerge therein in vain.
These dharmas are empty in nature and not real; Turning one's back on the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one clings to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Outwardly solid but inwardly hollow, one praises the virtues of others;

Perceiving objects, the mind arises and shifts again, deceiving the teacher and extinguishing the patriarchs while continuing old attachments. Pushing up from below and pulling down from above, one strives only for the heights.
A wind-crazed man of inverted views and contradictions; He claims his nature is extinguished and says he is an ordinary man possessed by ghosts.
All day long he studies prescriptions but refuses to take the medicine; His scattered thoughts and excessive greed leave him with a belly full of flaws.
There is no Buddha to be made once one merely pursues the mind; I urge people to eliminate doubt, and they will be equal to the Buddha.
Each person realizes the matter within their own heart; the mute man dreams but cannot speak it.
The Dharma-body eternally abides in the formless realm, its wondrous function radiating brilliance throughout the world.
That which is neither born nor extinguished is the rational nature (*li-xing*). This directly states and directly explains that sentient beings are fully endowed with the Dharma-body. True.
The wondrous nature of emptiness extends through all time, neither arising nor ceasing, unchanging and immovable, without coming or going, without old or new;
it is majestic and thus. The Most High said: "It is still and vast, standing alone and never altering."
It travels everywhere without weariness. It is also said: "Tranquil and unmoving, it responds and thereby penetrates all.

Thus, the four elements and five aggregates are left to their empty arising and empty passing away; they have no connection whatsoever with one's own *dharmakāya*. Now tell me: since there is no connection, what then?
"How can one remain undivided at every step? An ancient worthy said: "Harmonizing with the light, unstained by the dust; alone supreme within the three realms.
Master Chuan also said: "Where there is leisure, enjoy it; the clouds fly high and the waters flow on their own.
We see only the black winds tossing great waves, yet we have never heard of the fishing boat sinking. If this is so, tell me: is there any connection here?
There is no interaction. If one realizes that the five aggregates are all empty, what is there to be separated from or not separated from?
Do you understand? The flowing water never rests; the green mountains are ever tranquil. This single principle of true emptiness is attained spontaneously through non-action.
Neither born nor extinguished, one delights in joy; having attained the supreme shore, one chants "Ra-li";
upon the path of carefree wandering, one has emerged from the sea of suffering.
Xifang Road; Tianqiang Road; Anyi Main Road.
The Boundless Great Way;
the Home of Ultimate Bliss;
within the lands of all Buddhas.
Among the sages and worthies upon this earth, I have now attained the true meaning: to proclaim the scrolls, recite the Buddha’s name, and chant "Ra-li" is to be neither defiled nor pure.
It is also said that sentient beings are originally the pure Dharma-body; whether Buddha, person, ordinary being, or sage, they are ancient [and thus inherently pure].
Now, whether monk or layperson, male or female; birth or death, defilement or purity; increase or decrease, success or failure; heterodoxy or orthodoxy, good or evil; coming or going, fine or coarse;
light or dark, existence or non-existence; east, west, south, north; above, below, inside, or outside—none of these abide.
It is without name and without form; without trace and without flaw; without stain and without pollution; neither long nor short; neither square nor round; indestructible...
It can be attained; it cannot be burned. It is like empty space; it resembles a lotus flower that is neither stained by water nor is it pure.
It remains thus throughout all kalpas. Like the moon in the water, do you wish to see it? It radiates light wherever it is; how many people are able to see it?
To those who are willing to have faith, it constantly appears day and night.
Neither defiled nor pure, it maintains its own sovereignty; Nameless and signless, it is brilliantly luminous.
Abiding nowhere, it is unimpeded; Transverse and vertical, it moves with ease, radiating divine light.
Neither defiled nor pure—this is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); It does not abide in any extreme.
Not abiding in the Buddha, not abiding in the person, Mastery and freedom to know the causal person;
Clarify this phrase: within a single snap of the fingers, The great meaning of non-action suddenly awakens— Establishing one’s life and settling the self.
"Neither increasing nor decreasing" refers to the substance of the chaotic void and the body of the distant empty kalpa.
How could it increase? How could it decrease? The Way says: "In the sage there is no surplus; in the ordinary person there is no deficiency. The commentary says:
Suchness is spontaneous; it is neither deficient nor redundant. It is further said: "It endures through kalpas without decaying; it reaches back to antiquity without shifting. Yongjia said:
"Its essence is like space, without shore or limit; bodhisattvas of the highest vehicle believe this without doubt, while those of middle or lower capacity will surely find it strange.
But tell me, why is it so? Hehe! One's own tethering rope is too short—how could one possibly turn it around?
The well of resentment is deep. Having once known one another at the assembly on Vulture Peak, why do you fail to recognize me today?
It is precisely because you have been deluded by yourself; unaware and unawakened.
Neither increasing nor decreasing, there is no cultivation or realization; knowing the cause, one attains manifest perfection through faith.
Through skillful means, neither increasing nor decreasing, there is no cultivation or realization; by learning well, one attains manifest perfection through faith.
Virtuous One;
practicing the practices;
filial and obedient.
Advancing loyalty,
honoring the worthy and good,
and practicing impartiality.
The wealthy and noble,
the poor and lowly,
and the monastic and the lay.
Men and women;
old and young; soldiers;
Leisure and busyness;
the sick; the guilty.
Therefore, that which is "empty" refers to the wondrous Way of True Emptiness: neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure;
it cannot increase and cannot decrease. It is primordially pure, unchanged through past and present, eternally existing throughout ten thousand kalpas, and indestructible even by a blade.
An arrow cannot pierce it; a rope cannot bind it; fire cannot burn it; rain cannot moisten it; the sun’s heat cannot scorch it;
pushing or crowding it does not cause it to lean; striking it causes no pain; and grasping it is difficult to lift. Why is this so?

Because material objects do not obstruct empty space, and empty space does not obstruct material objects. The Immortal and Perfected One said: "True emptiness hangs upon nothing; the Great Way is untainted by dust."
The Old Man of the River said: "Empty space does not obstruct even a hair’s breadth of thought; therefore, he is manifest as the Great Awakened Immortal.
Thus, within emptiness, nature receives its mandate from Heaven; the Sage possesses the Way; having attained the Way, one returns to the primal source—the Lord Lao."
Śākyamuni Bodhisattva’s Path of Virtue;
Patriarchal Master.
Wisdom: knowing causes and conditions.
The Arhat of Merit has thoroughly penetrated it.
For a long time,
he clarified his mind and perceived his nature.
"Neither form, nor sensation, perception, mental formations, nor consciousness" expresses the aforementioned cause.

Since within emptiness there is the accumulation of the five aggregates, the substance of empty space accommodates form without receiving form; it accommodates sound without receiving sound; it accommodates sensation without receiving sensation;

it accommodates perception without receiving perception; it accommodates mental formations without receiving mental formations; and it accommodates consciousness without receiving consciousness. [The same applies to] the six realms and the four...
All produced provisional marks are entirely without acceptance. The pure, void, and wondrous Way does not admit even a speck of dust;
it is ultimately formless. Walking is like the path of a bird; sitting is like the great void. But tell me, how can one speak of the "bird-path" and the "great void"?
Though one walks the bird-path, no tracks are seen; though true emptiness is revealed, no signs are seen. Do you understand?

The five aggregates—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—are the sounds of Māra; Like silkworms spinning cocoons, they fall into the boiling cauldron, busily driven only by fame and profit.
Their thinking-mind acts as its own net, binding itself in self-imposed fetters.
Before one’s parents were born, there was not a single thing; Yet following the turbulent waves, one passes through the river of craving.
A single expanse of the sea of suffering surges with waves; The further one advances, the deeper one sinks without bottom.
On all sides are perilous terrains; It is solely because of coarse conduct that every step goes astray.
Be careful as you leave your native land; Since beginningless time, the karma created has been vast.
If you would escape saṃsāra and not undergo suffering, the great assembly should recite Amitābha’s name aloud.
If you would escape the four modes of birth and not incur retribution, fix your mind and keep Amitābha in your thoughts.
If you would escape the karma of birth and death within the six realms, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, recite Amitābha’s name.
If you would avoid coming and going within this Sahā world, recite the name of Amitābha every single morning.
If you would avoid the King of Yama’s face of cast iron, hear this early and turn toward the good, reciting the name of Amitābha.
That which has no eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, or mind is said to be the fundamental nature devoid of form and characteristics. Now tell me: what are these "no eyes, no ears"?
The nose, tongue, body, and mind—what are these? Cease looking, lest you miss them. I shall now explain clearly:
these six sense organs constitute the physical body; the absence of these six consciousnesses is called the Dharma-characteristic.
Such being the case, this is merely to instruct practitioners that although the eyes see, they must not become attached to forms; although the ears hear, they must not become attached to sounds.
Although the nose smells, do not become attached to fragrances or stenches. Although the tongue tastes, do not become attached to flavors.
Although one possesses a body, refrain from becoming attached to its form; you must forget both shape and substance. Although the mind responds to affairs, do not become attached to external objects;
it must remain constantly responsive yet constantly still. The Way says: "The eyes do not look at forms; the ears do not listen."

Regarding sound: the tongue does not crave flavors; the nose does not seek fragrances; the body does not move recklessly; and the mind is not deranged. The Confucian says: "Do not look at what is contrary to propriety;

do not listen to what is contrary to propriety; do not speak what is contrary to propriety; do not move in a way that is contrary to propriety. This is precisely to be without the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, body, and mind.
It is also the purification of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). It is to be unstained by the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). Furthermore, it is the six...
Consciousness is entirely empty. To speak of it in general terms, the eighteen realms are quiescent. It is also called the six depletions being extinguished and the six thieves dying;
the one true reality is unmoving, and the gates of the six senses are closed. To speak of it in general terms, the eighteen hells are empty. This is severance.
If it is thus, then paradise is near, and one immediately beholds the original *dharmakāya*. Do you wish to see the original *dharmakāya*? It is right here.
In the eye it is called seeing; in the ear, hearing; in the nose, smelling; in the tongue, speaking; in the hands, grasping; in the feet, running.

It is the entire body giving rise to function; it is the entire body as the *dharmakāya*. It is not merely the seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving of the six sense organs and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Cease identifying the four great elements and the six sense organs as yourself. As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "All that has marks is empty."
Wang Dao said: "The awakened forgets thoughts and returns to the truth; the deluded cling to appearances and lose their origin. All these are provisional names used to guide sentient beings;
they cannot be understood through mere intellectual grasp. One must personally see the Dharma-body.

If one attains such personal vision, one transforms from an ordinary person into a sage. To rely on the spoken words of others or to seek understanding through texts is like trying to satisfy hunger with a painted cake."
To say that wine quenches thirst is ultimately of no practical use. Xuanshi said: "Do not be vague regarding the medicinal flower in the railing;
the star is on the scale, not on the pan. Chongyang Zuoshi said: "Do not allow yourself to mistake the fixed star for the pan.

Now tell me, how should this phrase be explained? It is said that the pan can only hold equal weights; as for knowing lightness and distinguishing heaviness, all of that depends upon the star. Furthermore, the Patriarch...
I fear people will mistakenly fixate upon the "fixed point" (ding pansing). One must seek out the true fixed point;
yet even the fixed point is a dead thing, for it does not know lightness or heaviness. Therefore, do not allow yourself to mistakenly fixate upon the fixed point.
Generally, all are points: some are functional, while others are not. These are all metaphors for the Dharma. Examine them with meticulous care; do not cling to one side alone.
Now tell me, how is this principle? The true nature and the conscious nature, the true spirit and the conscious spirit—these dwell together as one;
one is false and one is real.
The Way lies within the ordinary activities of daily life; investigate and examine it through subtle contemplation.
Whether raising a hand or moving a foot, everything relies entirely upon the Way. In moments of leisure or busyness, whether in motion or stillness, the Way manifests before you.
With the eyes observing myriad objects and the ears hearing sounds and forms, [the Way is ever-present].
The nose smelling fragrance and stench; opening the mouth to speak and utter words;
eating food and wearing clothes; undergoing a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations;
maintaining the mind with patience; and reforming evil to turn toward the good.
Buying and selling, managing affairs; looking ahead and guarding behind.
When the Way supports one, the body is healthy; The hero and the eminent man have vigorous spirit.
When the Way is not present, the body has no master; The qi of the mandarin ducks is severed and cannot be beheld.
