At that time, all is ruined and difficult to cling to; scattered in five directions, one is bored by maggots.
Though you study the Way, you do not escape the suffering of birth and death. To be a person is to dwell in vain within the Southern Yamen;
borrow the false to cultivate the real, for the Real is eternally present—through ten thousand kalpas it never changes, regardless of the passing years.
That which is without form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or mental objects originally lacks the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). They all arise from a single faculty.
If one recognizes that consciousness arises from its fundamental source, that source is delusion; therefore, cease identifying with the sprouts. The Immortal Sage said:

"To stir the broth and extinguish the bubbles is not as good as pulling out the firewood from the bottom of the cauldron. The Buddha said: "If you wish to fell a tree, first remove its roots; the branches and twigs will fall of their own accord."
Having fallen [into realization], one recognizes the fundamental source; discarding the provisional, one returns to the true.

Recognizing that my own body does not exist—since even my own body is non-existent—all phenomena (*dharmas*) are empty and naturally pure. One contemplates the body as having no body, and contemplates phenomena as having no phenomena;

all return to emptiness and stillness, devoid of form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or mental objects (*dharmas*). My mind is fundamentally empty; neither sin nor merit has a master. What, then, is sin? What...
This is merit. A sutra says: "To contemplate clearly that the mind is originally empty—this is called true repentance.
But tell me, what is it that you repent? What is it that you regret? You repent for past transgressions and regret future faults.
Once the sense faculties have been severed, where can sprouts grow?
Without form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or phenomena—sweeping them clean, the flower of the mind appears before the eyes;
not loving form is "purity. From the sense-faculties, the flower of the mind surges forth;
the ears do not receive sounds.
The nose does not smell fragrances;
the tongue does not crave flavors;
the body does not touch forms.
The mind does not dwell on phenomena;
the six sense-objects do not enter, and there is no realm of Māra. The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom manifests as the flowers of the mind;
the six gates are level and penetrating, entirely without perception. The Wondrous Observational Wisdom manifests as the flowers of the mind.
The家风 (family tradition) of formlessness is fundamentally manifest; in the minds of all people, radiance breaks forth.
Opening wide the treasury of one's own spiritual powers, its enjoyment is inexhaustible. Those who transcend the world maintain their true will to fulfillment.
Establishing a firm foundation, they return to the source without deviation. Exhausting principle and perfecting nature, they abide in the stage of quiescent extinction.
I. The家风 (Family Style) of Formlessness: Who dares to uphold it? The sacred realm of True Emptiness cannot be reached except through no-conditions.
[From] the *Shentong Xian Dao Shenshen Gongde Baojuan*, Part I;
[From] the *Shentong Xian Dao Shenshen Gongde Baojuan*, Part II.
It is said: "There is no eye-element, and so on, up to no consciousness-element. These are originally formless. If the eye-element is purified, the consciousness-element becomes settled.
It is because of clinging to the existence of the eye that the eighteen elements are entangled and unsettled. Simply remove the eye-faculty and investigate its falsity.
An ancient worthy said: "The eye is a demonic army that obstructs the Way; by clinging to objects, one loses the way back home oneself. A Seer (Rishi) said: "The eye..."
Observe the movement of the mind: attachment to objects deludes one from the truth. This body will not endure long; the six sense faculties all return to decay and ruin.

When one quietly examines the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), they possess no substantial reality whatsoever. There exists only the wondrous nature of true emptiness, a substance that remains unimpaired through long kalpas, serene and eternally present, and requiring neither cultivation nor realization.
As the Śākya [Buddha] said: "The Nāga is always in samādhi; there is no time when it is not so maintained. Thus spoke my former teacher.
It is said: "The realm within meditative concentration; the universe within stillness. It is spontaneous and natural; it is not something produced by effort.

Once one has attained the power of concentration, how could there be any distraction? It is like the autumn moon—perfectly round and brilliantly shining, pervading heaven and earth, with no place that it does not illuminate.
Even to speak of 'illumination' is itself spontaneous, for it is not a product of deluded thought. —Shi.
Deyou also said: "My mind is not comparable to the moon; the moon has its waxing and waning. A single oilless lamp illuminates the ten directions through and through.
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth cannot obstruct it. Its radiance is brilliantly clear, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects.
Its essence reveals the true permanence; fundamentally, there is no defilement. Simply by being free from all conditions, one is an immortal and a Buddha."
There is no realm of the eye, and so on, up to emptiness;
there is no realm of consciousness from the very beginning, throughout vast kalpas, from Pangu until now.
Furthermore, there is neither "eye" nor "ear"—difficult to name, difficult to depict.
The nose, the tongue, the myriad sounds,
the body, and the mind— immeasurable and unfathomable,
without form or appearance, yet capable of transformation and possessing vast supernormal powers.
This true body is without comparison to the world: it is not a Buddha, not a human, not a sentient being,
not male or female, and neither ordinary nor holy.
Past and present are neither form nor emptiness—this wondrous meaning resides within every person. It is manifest all day long throughout the entire body;
yet though one searches minutely, its trace cannot be found.
Dark thoughts vanished; joy arose within my heart.
It was due to the compassionate mind of my teacher, who instructed me. Only then was I able to clearly request the Heart Sūtra;
He recited it once, and in every word I perceived the truth.
Discoursing on the wondrous Dharma, debating the infinite— Every word transcends the fundamental source, pure and naked;
Vividly clear, radiant light appears.
One is born without fear, Dies without sorrow, Possessing the indestructible golden body.
When there is no ignorance (*avidyā*), the myriad conditions do not arise. Ignorance is a dark, restless thought;
all sentient beings possess ignorance. Because of this ignorance, various distinctions and hundreds of afflictions (*kleśa*) arise—all of which are states of a dark and obscured mind.
It is for this reason that it is so. The Way says: "If the dark and obscured mind does not cease, one falls into the realms of hell and animals."
The *Ben* (Original) commentary states: "Ignorance fails to see the path to Bodhi; unaware, one casts the body into a pit of fire. The Confucians say:
"If the inch-sized mind is not obscured, the myriad dharmas are all clear. Furthermore, Guangchengzi said: "When wood is removed from fire, it does not turn to ash;
when a person removes their passions, they do not die. Taidian said: "The mind dwelling within the six senses is like a bird falling into a net; thus one creates sinful and evil karma."
Like moths rushing toward a lamp, or emerging from a shell only to enter another, they wander through kalpas without realizing it.

All this arises because of ignorance (*avidyā*). Because there is ignorance, there is volitional formation (*saṃskāra*); because of volitional formation, there is consciousness (*vijñāna*); because of consciousness, there is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);

because of name-and-form, there are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); because of the six sense bases, there is contact (*sparśa*); because of contact, there is feeling (*vedanā*); because of feeling, there is craving (*tṛṣṇā*); because of craving, there is grasping (*upādāna*). Because of...
Grasping leads to becoming; because of becoming there is birth; because of birth there is old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair—all of which have ignorance as their beginning.
Having directly perceived this ignorance here and now, I have subdued it and brought it to an end. With the death of death itself, all outflows are exhausted of their own accord.
Afflictions are forever severed; the three poisons extinguish themselves; the roots of evil are naturally removed. Cut straight to the source; do not look back at the branches and twigs.
If the root is severed, the branches and leaves wither of their own accord. When one no longer perceives a body, the body is exhausted and ignorance is exhausted; defilements are likewise exhausted.
The sins accumulated over ten thousand kalpas, as numerous as grains of sand, are all simultaneously and instantly stilled. The cycle of birth and death is, in an instant, utterly extinguished.
When ignorance is absent, the mind becomes clear and bright; one immediately knows where one has fallen, and simultaneously returns to the root;
one immediately knows the ultimate point.
The principle is clear and distinct;
one does not seek to cultivate merit,
nor does one crave the imperial palace.
Not seeking future lives;
not scheming for rebirth;
possessing a body entails suffering.
Not seeking a human body;
not scheming for marks;
the pure Dharma-body.
No ignorance; recognizing the other; the great road to the West;
the family style of signlessness;
what he loves is the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Establishing one's destiny and settling the self, yet there is none for whom ignorance is exhausted. This is the pure intention. When the principles are thoroughly mastered, delusion results in inverted false conceptualization.

This is the mind whose karma is ignorance; when awakened, it transforms the ordinary into the sagely. This is the perfectly luminous nature of awareness (*bodhi*). It is all one and the same ground of the mind;
there is only a distinction between clarity and lack of clarity. The Supreme One said: "They emerge from the same source yet have different names.
Yongjia said: "The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; the illusory and empty body is itself the Dharma-body. If one clings to this illusory body as being the self, then...

There is ignorance; there is ignorance, which immediately gives rise to the three poisons and initiates the three types of evil karma. These three karmas cause darkness and confusion, rendering the six sense faculties internally blind.
Consequently, one fails to awaken or realize the truth, turning one's back on enlightenment and uniting with the sensory dust, thereby falling into the three evil realms.
Just as a person possessing wisdom can transform a mind of stinginess and greed into a mind of joyful relinquishment, and transform a mind of anger into a mind of joy, so too [can one transform...]
The mind that clings with ignorance is transformed into a mind of harmonious liberation. The six thieves are changed into the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
When one undergoes this single or double transformation, one naturally shifts from the mundane to the sacred; the ordinary person is itself the sage.
If one cannot effect this transformation or achieve this change, the sage is itself the ordinary person. How can it be that the ordinary person is turned by external objects, while the sage is not?
If a person can transform things, the common people use them daily without realizing it. All day long they are in a state of frantic bustle, led astray by external objects.
As days turn into months and months into years, they become increasingly distant from their home and fail to return; thus they lose the truth and forget their origin.

If one understands that the myriad phenomena all return to oneself, how could one ever lose the true source? The Old Man of Chuan said: "All day long they are in a state of frantic bustle—what [is this]?"

There is no hindrance in these matters. Seek not liberation; take no pleasure in the heavenly realms. If you can but for a single thought-moment return to non-thought, you shall stride with lofty steps upon the crown of Vairocana’s head.
The Way says: "Dwelling in the dust, one is not stained by the dust; abiding in desire, one is without desire. Body and mind are as they are (*tathatā*);
internally and externally, there is nothing remaining. You must achieve this as a single whole, equal to the kalpa of emptiness, where form and shadow do not exist—this is the reversal.
Contemplating one's own body: my body is not real; all else is empty. My body is but a provisional construct, yet it possesses profound ignorance.
When ignorance is exhausted, all things are severed. The iron face is devoid of sentiment; there is no need to speak of mysterious and subtle dharmas.
Not even a breath of wind can penetrate it. The principle of non-action is most stern and urgent.
Ignorant sentient beings labor in vain, Gathering in a profusion of scattered thoughts; it would be better to read the sutras with simple devotion.
Failing to understand the intent of the Tathāgata, Their mouths recite while their hearts remain in opposition, and their minds lack penetration.
Bound by a continuous chain of delusive thoughts, They pluck leaves and seek branches without ever resting.
Reverently serve the Honored Teacher and guard the root source; Suddenly eliminate doubt, and you will be truly pure and clear.
In a fleeting glance, know the essential point thus; The Buddhas and Patriarchs all speak in this way.
If you can believe even a single phrase of the Heart Sutra, A snap of the fingers brings clarity and transcends the triple world.
"Up to and including the absence of old age and death. For one who practices the Way, it is necessary to forget the illusory form and discard the physical body.
Since the self-body does not exist, how can there be ignorance? Since ignorance does not exist, birth and death are also severed.
The Supreme One said: "Internally observing the mind, the mind has no mind; externally observing the form, the form has no form; observing objects from afar, the objects have no objects. (Three)
Once one has attained awakening, one perceives only emptiness. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"There is no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient being, and no mark of life-span. When these three are absent, all four marks are empty. What ignorance or old age and death could there be?
All phenomena are inherently empty; this itself is the immortal and the Buddha. Yet even these two words, "immortal" and "Buddha," are superfluous—they are merely forced designations.

Name. Furthermore, sentient beings are inverted; deluded by the illusory phenomena before their eyes and led astray by habitual tendencies, they are like shifting forms and shadows, unable to act as masters.
They flow along with worldly objects, and because they cling to a self, their deluded minds do not cease.

Failing to eliminate the distinction between self and others, they become attached to sounds and forms, falling into the cycle of birth and death. If one is a person who has seen their nature, there is no dharma before their eyes, nor—
There are no sentient beings. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. In the equal and true Dharma-realm, they are observed as a single essence.
The myriad dharmas return to the One. But how can they be observed as one? The Immortal Sage said: "Though the branches may differ slightly, the root is not distinct.
Though the streams diverge into various branches, the hundred rivers still return to the sea. Furthermore, before the Great Ultimate (Tàijí) was divided, all was a chaotic unity."
The One Qi—how could there be two? Once heaven and earth were divided, there arose high and low. One gives birth to Two; Two gives birth to Three;
Three gives birth to the myriad things—all are transformations of the One Qi. Heaven is this Dao; Earth is this Dao; Humanity is this Dao.
Whether sentient or insentient, all are born from the Qi of the Dao. When observing the minor details, the myriad species appear unequal; yet knowing [the source], they are one.
At the fundamental level, there is no distinction whatsoever. The Immortal and Perfected One said: "That which is equal and non-dual is the man of complete perfection.
If one thoroughly understands this principle, then when there is birth, one follows it in being born; when there is aging, one follows it in aging; when there is illness, one follows it in illness;
and when there is death, one follows it in dying. Birth, aging, sickness, and death have never interfered with or affected me. Like bubbles arising—
The bubble vanishes. The waves roll and surge; this is the constant nature of water. Dadian said: "One who has reached the home of reality sees neither birth and death, nor arising and ceasing.
Heavens and hells, the six realms and four modes of birth—all are illusory transformations.
To one who has reached the bottom, none of these have any connection whatsoever. Naturally, they let go of their entire being. An ancient said: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent."
All is empty; this is the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment.
Even unto old age and death, there is nothing. Since beginningless time, it has never existed as a primordial portion within Jambudvīpa, nor does it possess an inherent nature.
This nature is the Tathāgata’s immeasurable life-span.
The cycles of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness pass through countless eons; the rotation of heaven and earth is beyond calculation.
Within emptiness forms manifest, yet these forms are subject to decay. Emptiness is the infinite, the firm and enduring;
before heaven and earth existed, emptiness was already present. Emptiness gives birth to Yin and Yang; emptiness is the Mother.
Deluded people do not understand the meaning of the primordial source; alas, these disciples have coarse minds and natures.
With large mouths and long tongues, they boast of their ability to comprehend, deceiving their teachers and showing contempt for the scriptures.
They slay the Buddhas and Patriarchs, rejecting the subduing of heterodoxy and the manifestation of the orthodox. Clinging to mud and water, they are no true men of integrity.
Even until there is no more aging or long life, Neither born nor extinguished, like an immortal;
When the time arrives and conditions converge, One returns from delusion to truth and enters the source.
It is largely due to the True and Wondrous Dharma of the Patriarchs, Which has exposed past causes and brought one out of the cycle of suffering.

I have now attained the Way and found a place of peace for my person; mind after mind, thought after thought, I never forget the debt of gratitude. Furthermore, there is no one who has exhausted old age and death.
Since there is neither old age nor death, it remains thus throughout eternal kalpas; how could it ever come to an end? That which has an end is the physical body;
that which is free from old age and death is the true mark of the empty Dharma. Thus, I neither cling to existence nor am I obstructed by emptiness; I live.
It is surging and vibrant; it turns and rolls; it is perfectly round; it is brilliantly radiant—how could there ever be an end to it?

A practitioner of the Way must first strike it clean and clear before there can be a point of resonance. The Supreme Lord said: "Diminish it again and diminish it until one reaches non-action (*wuwei*);
though in a state of non-action, do not cease acting. Dadian said: "One who studies the Way is like one peeling..."
It is like a plantain tree: peel away one layer after another until there is nothing left to grasp.

Naturally, you will return to the source and restore the origin, attaining the emptiness of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). It is as if they had never arisen; it is as if they had been completely incinerated.

Reaching the state where emptiness is not empty, the entire body is utterly forgotten, leaving no trace behind. One must possess the eyes and hands of the whole body, without establishing even a speck of dust.

Names and words—how much more so the twelve links of dependent origination? The six perfections, the myriad practices, and the ascetic dhūta observances are all suddenly cast off at once, like withered wood or extinguished ashes;
it is as if there were not one person present in a hundred. As the ancients said: "It is not a matter of washing the heart to eliminate delusive thoughts;
it is simply because there is nothing to be pondered. If one further speaks of birth and death, of cause and effect, or of...
To speak of the nature of the mind is to be bound by phenomena. Yongjia said: "The mind is the root; phenomena are the dust. These two are like blemishes upon a mirror.
When the stains of these blemishes are completely removed, the light finally appears. When both mind and phenomena are forgotten, one enters the city of Nirvana."
There is neither aging nor death, nor any vulgar sentiments; it has been thus throughout vast eons—how could it ever end?
Without obstruction in the four directions, all are observed as one body; what need is there for much talk?
The Dharma-body universally covers the great chiliocosm, within the merged source of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time all abide in the Way; Their fundamental nature is interconnected like the great void.
Each person must realize the matter within their own heart; When a thousand lamps illuminate a single room, their light is undivided.
Mindfully repay the kindness of the enlightened teacher—difficult to requite; Without falling into dualistic discrimination, repay the grace of the Patriarchs.
Having reached the shore, one has never used a boat; The level Great Way penetrates eternal peace.
Knowing clearly that awakening does not depend on another, The true face is distinct and always the same.
Three before and three after— Any deliberation or calculation is utterly unfit.
Even if you were to sever both consciousness and emotion, Re-examine this single segment of life through three births and nine kalpas;
it is not contained within the six realms. All phenomena of the past are entirely peerless;
With a light stroke, he splits asunder the three thousandfold world-system, Until even the waters of the Ganges flow upward.
Regarding "there being no suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path": once one has forgotten the physical form, birth and death are immediately severed and can never again be exhausted.
How could there then be suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path? A former master said: "Because of having body and mind, one invites manifold sufferings;
if one can forget body and mind, how can suffering arise? The commentary states: "The body is the root of all suffering; the mind is the source of evil karma. If one can let go...
Lowering body and mind, one then ascends to the other shore of Bodhi. Dadian said:

"For those of the Lesser Vehicle who practice the six perfections and myriad deeds with diligence day and night, yet seek the Dharma outside the mind—there is no such place where they can escape these Four Noble Truths, leave the world, or escape saṃsāra.
The Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of the Great Matter; they do not deliver beings by means of the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle."

Regarding sentient beings, those who follow the Mahāyāna study the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Sitting upright, they contemplate the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). All transgressions are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can eliminate them.
Abiding in a secluded place, they collect and withdraw their minds. Sitting upright and motionless, they observe that all phenomena (*dharma*) are utterly non-existent.
Looking back upon the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), they see that the body is not the essence of awakening. Only through signlessness (*animitta*) is the truth revealed.

One knows for oneself that it is empty and still. Suddenly one contemplates the purity and exhaustion—the function of non-action that is yet efficacious. Unbroken through long kalpas, this is the action of non-action, wherein one does not act.
It is suchness, immovable; profound and eternally tranquil. As the Lotus Sūtra says: "All dharmas from the very beginning are always of the nature of quiescent extinction.
When the Son of the Buddha has practiced the Way, he shall become a Buddha in a future age, adorned with the power of concentration and wisdom. Without...
There is delusion but no awakening. There is neither suffering nor pleasure. There is neither stillness nor extinction. There is neither the Way nor attainment.

There is neither wisdom nor loss. Originally there is not a single thing; even the bright mirror is not a stand. Reaching this point, cultivation and realization are non-existent, and defilement cannot take hold.
To leap directly into the stage of the Tathāgata—does one need to "see" the Tathāgata? The Tathāgata seems to come but does not come; seems to go but does not go.
If you try to send him away, he cannot be found; if you try to detain him, he does not remain.
Suffering is absent where there is quiescent extinction and the path has reached its end; without merit and without sin, one is released from the cage of the mundane.
Having forgotten the physical form, birth and death are severed, and one attains the indestructible Vajra body.
Since it is because of having a body and mind that one invites manifold sufferings, once the body and mind are forgotten, how could suffering arise?
Not seeking the human body, severing birth and death; not seeking to become a Buddha, escaping the cage of the mundane;
nor seeking the fruits of immortals, bodhisattvas, or arhats.
Casting aside greed, one ascends to the other shore; turning one's back on the dust of the world and uniting with awakening, the Way is truly realized.
By not abiding in dharmas, one transcends birth and death; returning from delusion to truth, the Way is perfected.
Those of the Lesser Vehicle refuse to cultivate merit; detesting poverty and loving wealth is a great deluded mind.
Cultivating [virtue] brings immeasurable merit in future lives; Relying on wealth to deceive the poor gathers the roots of karma.
Yama the King is incensed, and the Buddha does not rejoice; Where could such a person find peace?
If one wishes to escape the suffering of saṃsāra, It is like a donkey growing horns or a jar sprouting roots.
"Neither wisdom nor attainment" means that since even one's own body is merely provisional, how could there be any attainment? Daowu said: "In reality, there is nothing attained;
it is for the sake of transforming sentient beings that it is called 'attaining the Way. The commentary says: "There is neither person nor Buddha;
the great trichiliocosm is but bubbles on water; all sages and worthies are like a flash of lightning. It further says: "It is not mind, not Buddha, not [the scriptures]."
Regarding "objects," Dadian said: "When one reaches such a state, it is like a thief entering an empty house;

there is nothing to steal. The *Daodejing* says: "To be free from all extremes is called the wondrous Way. The commentary explains: "The self-nature is pure; in reality, not a single dharma can be grasped by the mind.
From the beginning, there is the 'bestowal of dharmas,' yet upon bestowal, there are no dharmas at all. Each person awakens to this within their own mind; once awakened, there is nothing [to grasp]."

There is no dharma. There is no gain and no loss; no progress and no cultivation. If there is even the slightest trace within the breast, there will be gain and loss, "I can" and "I know," "I have awakened" and "I answer," "I am clever" and "I possess wisdom"—all of these are instances of *adhimāna* (arrogance).
If one does not eliminate the sense of self and other, one falls entirely into birth and death. If one is a person of true realization, it is altogether not like this; they naturally transcend it.
The Path of the Body. Now tell me, what is the path for emerging from the body? Strike it until the four quarters are pure;
then you may proceed forward with ease. Originally, this has not a speck of dust; one only fears that people mistake the true for the false.
Having let go, there is nothing at all; where is there not the ancient style? (Wulingchun)
The ignorant person cannot find a way to escape this body;
they spend their whole life in busyness, throwing a lifetime into chaos, only to return once more to the dark realms of the underworld.
Day after day, the ignorant person does nothing but commit evil.
Impermanence arrives; birth and death reach us. There is no door on the path where living beings are harmed.
Fearing the killing-demons who pursue one's life, if you do not believe in the Buddha and do not believe in the Dharma, you should contemplate the sutras.
The ignorant person constantly recollects the Buddha, yet does not know that when they reach the brink of peril, there is nowhere to flee; where can such a one find refuge?
The ignorant person knows how to chant the sutras, yet does not understand the meaning of the Buddha’s teachings.
Relying on a strong heart, not consulting a teacher, such a person of no wisdom passes an entire life in vain.
Relying on appearances, they fail to distinguish the true from the false;
when facing a crisis, they find nothing to rely upon—exerting themselves in labor yet achieving no merit.
The ignorant person does not contemplate the good;
They clamor for fame and seize profit, deceiving their own minds, And betraying the principles of Heaven. Sinful karma follows them wherever they go.
The ignorant person feasts on delusion, Refusing to investigate the Way.
The Buddha does not rejoice, and the spirits and deities are angered;
there is no place to escape from the causes created in this life or the conditions for future lives.
Yet, by meeting the assembly of Buddhas and planting roots of goodness, and by encountering the True Dharma, one may likewise attain rebirth.
Leaving behind children and grandchildren, casting aside family ties, and severing human affections, one undergoes the karma of the lower realms and goes to suffer. Who knows this gratitude?
Because there is "nothing to be attained," that which is attained is non-attainment; it is the single essence of emptiness and voidness. When a practitioner reaches this point, [they realize this].
Regarding the stages of entering the Mahāyāna: sentient beings revolve in the cycle of birth and death because they cannot find rest;

this is due to their failure to see their true nature and their lack of wisdom, which prevents them from extensively awakening to the meaning of immeasurable emptiness, causing them instead to cling to the intellectual understandings within their own minds.
One’s original mind is thereby lost. Dadian said: "That which enters from without is not one's own family treasure. Xianzhen said:

"To study the words within another's mind is ultimately to speak the language of another. Sentient beings, deluded by extensive learning and intellectual understanding based on dry wisdom, accumulate these habits in their hearts until they become arrogant.
An ancient said: "If there is even a hair’s breadth [of it], it is dust. If this dust is not eliminated, one knows only..."

Regarding the matter of legendary accounts: if the dust of delusion is completely exhausted, one will personally perceive all objects and personally know all phenomena, just as a person with clear vision ascending a high mountain sees everything without exception.
A practitioner must reach the ultimate limit where the present coincides with the empty kalpa (*śūnya-kalpa*), not falling into secondary views.
Only by returning to the root and attaining the essential meaning will there be true resonance. If one is attached to the self and others, one will instead give rise to contempt and negligence.
The Bhikṣu Shanxin lectured on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, yet his arrogance increased and he failed to eliminate the sense of self; consequently, he was reborn and fell into hell.
Dharma Master Yun Guang lectured on the same sūtra until heavenly flowers rained down in profusion, yet he did not reform his greed and anger and fell into the realm of oxen.

If one wishes to transcend the Buddhas and Patriarchs, one must maintain a state of emptiness and stillness in every thought-moment. The world is an illusory transformation; all are but adventitious defilements. Only the Great...
The substance of emptiness does not harbor sound or form, nor does it allow even a speck of dust to stand; it is like space itself.
Such a person is one who has understood the matter—a practitioner of purity and peace.
Because there is nothing to be gained, one is unable [to practice]; One is unwilling to learn and instead delights in being an evildoer.
Time is limited; how many more days can there be? Suddenly, impermanence brings one into the dark realm of the underworld.
Ten thousand bolts of silk in wealth cannot be taken along; Relatives and kinsmen leave no trace behind.
Friends and brothers cannot look upon one another; Wives, concubines, sons, and daughters are likewise empty.
The Unconstantant Ghost of Death comes to claim one's life; Thousand-headed horse-faced demons do not let go.
Once entered the Hall of the Thousandfold Net in the Underworld, King Yama is enraged, his breath fierce and surging.
Though you come and go as you please, I spare your life; I send you back to the world of the living to practice cultivation, yet you remain unvirtuous in your conduct.
The Buddha’s words were like the wind passing by one's ear;
you cast them aside, betraying kindness and virtue, and refusing to hold me accountable. Now I deliver you to the Avīci Hell for you to experience its retribution.
The rocks have crumbled away and the mustard seeds are exhausted; when the three calamities have ended, one merely turns over.
"Bodhisattva" is a term from the Sanskrit of the Western Heavens; in this Eastern Land, it is translated as "emptiness of persons and emptiness of phenomena.
Dadian said: "To fully realize the emptiness of persons is called *bodhi*; to fully realize the emptiness of phenomena is called *sattva*. When both person and phenomenon are...

Emptiness is called Wondrous Enlightenment. If those of the Small Vehicle who have attained the four fruits adhere to signs in their practice, performing diligent and ascetic austerities until they cultivate the untainted state (*anāsrava*), sever the dust-like delusions, and bring their fruit and conduct to perfection—attaining the fruit of an Arhat—they are like a deer leaping alone.
Their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are narrow and inferior; they fall among the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, unable to receive sentient beings or benefit living things. If...
If one does not see one's nature, one cannot attain the stage of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching. It is essential to see one's nature;

if one attains this vision of nature, one transforms from an ordinary person into a sage in the space of a finger-snap. Spontaneously, through karmic conditions, one awakens to the Buddha’s samādhi and knows the source of the Great Way.

Although there is no teacher-wisdom, natural wisdom abounds. Through various skillful means, one delivers all who are deluded and leads them to awakening, so that they may together ascend to the other shore. Furthermore...
Not receiving birth; a separate transmission outside the teachings. Entering the Dharma-gate of perfect and sudden non-obstruction. Now tell me, what is this Dharma-gate of non-obstruction?
It is like a level plain where one traverses the seven paths and penetrates the eight directions.
Bodhisattvas are empty of both person and phenomena; there is nothing to cultivate and nothing to realize, yet they manifest the perfection of *bodhicitta*.
When Bodhisattvas come to bear witness, how could there be five schools or three sects?
A Bodhisattva is not a single thing at all; every day, one remains serene—*cīlūṭu*.
Observe the full moon on the fifteenth night: The myriad stars are bright, yet the moon stands alone.
Whether the Bodhisattva is empty or not empty, He shatters error and reveals realization, radiating light.
The worlds of atoms cannot compare; The person of original nature is difficult to depict or paint.
In the Bodhisattva, person and dharmas have vanished; Before the Grand Ultimate (*tàijí*), there was not a single thing.
From the Infinite transformations, the Two Polarities were born; The Five Elements divided the Great Ultimate Diagram.
The Bodhisattva is likewise empty; Recognize the source and do not follow your passions.
The man himself possesses wisdom that pierces the heavens; He does not walk where the Tathāgata has walked.
Space neither increases nor decreases; That which neither increases nor decreases is my own body.
All phenomena do not occupy the nature of space; In the emptiness of nature, there is no occupation by worldly dust.
Regarding the phrase "By virtue of the *prajñāpāramitā*," these six intermediate characters are explained according to the various interpretations mentioned previously.
By practicing [this], one attains great wisdom; having attained wisdom, one will surely reach the other shore (*pāra*). Furthermore, it is the most honored and supreme within the great void;
this awakened nature of *prajñā* is such that nothing in heaven or on earth can equal it. The Way says: "Ten days have passed."

It is better to practice non-action for a single day than [to learn for a year]. It is also said: "To study the teachings for one year is not as good as attaining the Way for a single day. An ancient worthy said:
"To study the Dharma for a thousand days is not as good as studying Prajñā for a single day. Dadian said: "Prajñā penetrates the Great Treasury of Radiance;
it is like a person entering the ocean—the deeper they enter, the deeper it becomes. Thus one hears the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and awakens to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

He possesses great supernormal powers and manifold transformations; through skillful means, he manifests various forms to benefit beings according to their capacities, never falling into a secondary state.
He contemplates all as a single essence within the equal and true Dharma-realm, where there are no sentient beings to be saved and no Buddha to be made.
Do you understand this principle? Though rivers flow in different branches, they share the same source upon reaching the sea.
The Perfection of Wisdom is perfected; The long-suffering eyes find peace in that moment.
Truly deficient in the true Dharma-words of a clear master, The body becomes light and agile, the mind-ground expansive.
Encountering the Buddha’s samādhi clarifies the rational nature; Hearing the Buddha’s samādhi, one recognizes the source.
Awakening to the Buddha’s samādhi possesses merit; The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) samādhi attains spontaneous *mārga*.
Unconditioned, yet there is nothing it does not do; The principle of the unconditioned is universally one and the same.
Sentient beings possess this portion and have the requisite conditions; Having lost their home for countless kalpas, they now regain it.
Profoundly awakening to the boundless, primordial nature, One lightly leaps through the barrier of birth and death.
When Prajñā manifests before one, there is no hindrance; Transcending the universe, do not harbor doubt or suspicion.
The void is squeezed through, impossible to conceal or hide; The Great Way is clearly revealed—return! Return!
Neither coming nor going, and likewise formless; Entering and exiting, yet mistakenly taking the crosshair for the compass point.
How excellent is this Dharma of sovereign, true emptiness! To return to the root and restore the source is the ancient family style of one whose mind is free from hindrance.
Such a person immediately awakens to the wondrous principle of true emptiness; it is vast and penetrating like the great void, pure and inherently so, eternally present.
Attaining mastery, the Immortal Sage said: "If the mind is like the great void, it is unstained by a single thing. The Commentary says: "The mind is identical to the realm of empty space;
you yourselves are the dharma of empty space. When one realizes empty space, there is neither 'is' nor 'is not.

Since it has merged into a single essence with empty space, what differentiation can there be? What is right and what is wrong? Internally and externally pure; internally empty and externally [empty]."
Emptiness. Its very substance is emptiness. Before heaven and earth existed, this emptiness already existed. The Most High said:
"There was something formless and complete, born before heaven and earth. He further said: "Nameless is the beginning of heaven and earth;

named, it is the mother of the myriad things. It cannot be seen when looked at, nor heard when listened to; one cannot grasp it. When met from the front, its head is not seen; when followed from behind, it is not seen.
Thereafter, the Five Eyes could not fully trace its tracks, and the Two Hearings ceased to hear its resonance. Chuanlao said: "The majestic Great Way is brilliant and distinct;
it is inherently possessed by every person and perfectly realized by each individual. It is only because of a single mistaken thought that ten thousand forms manifest.
The Sixth Patriarch said: "I have an object that reaches up to heaven and down to earth; no one recognizes it."
If you personally behold even one aspect of it, you will surpass all Buddhas and patriarchs, transcend the three realms, and not fall into saṃsāra.
For yourself, you must be willing and have self-confidence; thus you will attain the unimpeded Dharma, certain and without obstruction. Do you understand?
Tear apart the net that covers the heavens, remove the boulder blocking the path; because of this, there is no hindrance. Today, at last, the time has come.
With a mind free from obstruction, one realizes that delusive conditions are empty;
Having discerned through insight that the dusty world is irrelevant, one contemplates all insentient things to their end. When attachment and affection are severed, spontaneity is attained;
Knowing the cause, one does not seek the realm of the Western Land, for the Pure Land is originally the formless heaven.
The ten directions are all the realm where Buddhas walk; The pure Dharma-body is vast and boundless. Beholding it, one sees nothing;
it has no form or appearance. Listening, one hears nothing; it is empty and beyond words.
Seeking it, one finds nothing; it is profound and wondrous. Yet its head follows along, appearing before one’s very eyes.
The majestic Great Way is constantly visible to my face; Its brilliant majesty clearly illuminates the great thousandfold world.
I have now attained the Way of the Infinite; This was largely due to the enlightened Master who escorted me through the pass.
I have found the place where I may dwell in peace.
To "attain the vision of the Mother of Non-arising" and "recognize one's own true face" means that because there is no obstruction,
both the internal and external are pure, and all conditions are cast off. It is like the brilliant sun shining in a clear sky, its light—
It fills the great trichiliocosm, illuminating everything without exception. All illusory realms are entirely free from obstruction.
To the east it extends infinitely; to the west it reaches the utmost limit. Moving freely in all directions, it cannot be constrained by illusory phenomena.

This is the fundamental source-nature, the innate and natural body that remains undestroyed through long kalpas—without going or coming, without change or variation. When the mist clears, the sun reveals itself of its own accord.

When the dust is cleared, the mirror is naturally bright; thus, the single character "hence" (故) carries the meaning of perfection. The ultimate limit is likewise the principle of true permanence, which cannot be expressed in words.
Because it cannot be spoken, it is called "hence. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "There is no dharma that can be taught;
this is called teaching the Dharma. The Confucians say: "The Way is fundamentally wordless; to open one's mouth is to lose the principle. The Immortal Master said: "The Way is fundamentally..."
Difficult to explain; one must awaken to it for oneself. A single strike on the golden bell resounds; from the high tower, the drum beats (awakening those within a dream).
Originally empty and without obstruction, one becomes deluded by clinging to forms. If a person can turn back [from this delusion], they will be equal to the immortals and Buddhas.
Unobstructed, its nature is emptiness;
how could there be such a teaching of quiescent extinction? It is difficult to awaken to.
Many do not apply their minds in the manner required for investigation. Observe closely; you must reach the ultimate bottom.
Knowing lightness and heaviness, distinguishing black from white, naturally clear and distinct—
neither thinking of the present nor thinking of the past, the mind is free from obstruction; whether human or Buddha,
day and night there is peace and tranquility.
The mental phenomena of ordinary beings and sages,
whether good or evil thoughts occurring during the day.
Cultivation, realization, day, formation, destruction,
mind, preference, reversal, day.
Precepts, discipline, mind, existence, non-existence, day—
these things are originally non-existent and cannot be grasped.
Having laid down all phenomena, one moves with sovereign ease and freedom, free from fear.
Since the mind is without obstruction, it is truly, eternally, and spontaneously perfect; what further cause for fear could there be?
Upon reaching this state, one realizes the emptiness of intrinsic nature, such that east and west are no longer distinguished, nor are north and south.

Not deceived by light or darkness, not obstructed by the corners of the world, not constrained by yin and yang, and not enslaved by the forces of creation—being thus, what sorrow, suffering, or dread could there be? What birth and death could be feared?
Not associating with the myriad dharmas, one always walks and strides alone. Looking up, one ascends to heaven without end; entering the earth, one goes beyond.
It is boundless. Mountains, rivers, rocky cliffs, earth, water, fire, and wind—coming and going through these, there is no obstruction whatsoever.
One can walk a thousand li with the palm of one’s hand turned sideways; returning, it is like flying. Neither heaven nor earth can restrain it;

neither spirits nor ghosts can fathom it. This is called the Great Awakened Golden Immortal. What is it? There is no need to seek it with torches or lamps; it is constantly present as you drink when thirsty and eat when hungry.
The face is free from fear; the mind is expansive and clear, free from fear; no objects are grasped;
defiled dharmas are extinguished; and one is not deceived.
The waves have ceased; free from inversion, one emerges from the sea of suffering. At the edge of the further shore, there is no fear;
one clarifies the great meaning. Without fear, one arrives at the Land of Peaceful Nourishment.
In the heart there is joy; one attains spontaneity;
There is the bliss of carefree wandering; one enjoys constancy;
Body and life are secure; one does not fall into partiality.
One may be satisfied and thank the heavens:
the Pure Land of the West belongs to every person. Without relying on cultivation, it is already manifest before us.
If all superior and virtuous people see their true nature, they shall stand shoulder to shoulder with Amitābha Buddha.
"Far removed from inverted dreams and delusions": if one is free from attachment and devoid of fear, one will naturally be far removed from inverted dreams and delusions.
The Immortal Master said: "During the day there are no discursive thoughts; after nightfall, dreams are few. The Commentary says:

"Dreams arise because of thoughts; thoughts arise because of dreams. Worldly people know only that there are dreams when the eyes are closed, but they do not realize that there are also dreams when the eyes are open."

"What is it like to have a dream while one's eyes are open? The Immortal Master said: "Even if gold and silver pass beyond the Northern Dipper, when the great limit arrives, it is all within a single dream.
Is this not dreaming even with one's eyes open? If you wish for the dream to awaken, you must wait until impermanence strikes."
One then reflects upon all that was done, done for, craved, and loved during one's life; all myriad conditions are but a single spring dream.
Even this single body of one’s own can no longer be sustained. When one realizes this, it is already too late.
If a person of wisdom suddenly attains self-reflection and self-awakening, realizing that impermanence has arrived, then all these cravings, desires, and attachments will utterly vanish.
This is the seed of saṃsāra, the cause of the hells. To distance oneself from inversion and awaken to the emptiness of one's original nature, one realizes that this body is necessarily non-existent.
As the ancients said: "The sage has no intention and no fixedness; no necessity and no self; no dependence and no leaning;
no obscurity and no brightness; no form and no name; no strength and no weakness; no defilement and no purity; no cessation and no action. No...
Renunciation is non-extinction. It is without silence and without speech; it cuts off thought and eliminates deliberation.
All paths of language are severed, and the sphere of mental activity ceases. Dàshàng said: "In truth, there is nothing to be attained, yet one acts for the sake of transforming sentient beings.

The commentary states: "The Way is subtle and profound, such that it cannot be seen. Dàdiān said: "When dead and cremated, there is neither hunger nor thirst, neither cold nor heat, neither arising nor..."
It is overturned. There is no sitting and no sleeping; there are no six sense organs, no nine apertures, no four hundred and four diseases, and no eighty-four thousand worms.
It is forever free from inversion. If one does not awaken in this way, within the pure realm, a single thought-moment is already eight thousand years in Jambudvīpa.
If you realize it, it is in a single *kṣaṇa*; if you do not realize it, it is for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Death after death, life after life.
Passing from one state to another without awareness, one sleeps through long dreams without awakening; for ten thousand kalpas, one remains inverted and without end.

Invert after inversion, one dies again and is born, and is born again and dies; from dream to dream, and from waking to sleep, one becomes more deluded within delusion, with no time of final liberation.
If there is someone who can strike through to the bottom and pass beyond, they will forever be exempt from such inversion.
Stay far removed from delusions; do not look back even slightly. Guard the foundation of your own nature firmly.
By committing no evil, the mountains of sin and the oceans of karma will vanish all at once.
Mundane sentiments will recede, and no karmic conditions whatsoever shall be able to bind you.
When the deluded mind ceases, demonic realms naturally vanish;
when attachment is severed, one is liberated from shackles with joyous ease.
When the mind is luminous and clear, the floating clouds part and the light shines forth brilliantly.
Not following after signs; shattering delusions to reveal the wisdom of realization, the measure of knowledge is lofty;
free from the attachment to dharmas; though obstructed by worlds as numerous as motes of dust, there is no clinging;
in the cycle of birth and death, who can escape? If this mind is not yet understood, one toils in the path of arrogance.
Now, at this time, do not dream of saṃsāra; simply traverse this single journey through the human realm and realize ultimate nirvāṇa.
Turn inward and investigate your own body: it is entirely false and illusory. In a single day, impermanence will strike and all shall fall into ruin;
it is difficult to harbor attachment to such things. To reach such a realization is sufficient. Originally, these four elements did not exist.

Because all people in the world cling to the existence of a self, they are deluded regarding their own nature and pursue external objects; they abandon kin for strangers and mistake a thief for a son.
They falsely take the four elements and six sense organs to be real, thereby performing various karmas and undergoing various sufferings.

For ten thousand kalpas they transmigrate in samsara, neither awakening nor realizing [the truth], and thus unable to attain liberation. Reflect silently upon this within yourself, day and night, never departing from the present moment. From yourself—
Awaken to self-illumination. Investigate minutely: these six sense faculties and five aggregates have, since time immemorial, been fundamentally nameless and formless from the beginning;
they are entirely unattainable. There is no becoming an immortal or a Buddha, nor are there the six realms or the four modes of birth;
all such things are utterly unattainable. "Jing" (竟) means "exhaustion. Upon reaching this point, all is uniformly equal; everything is overturned to its very bottom.
All conditions suddenly cease; there is nothing remaining within or without. Master Chuanshuo said: "It is like cutting a handful of silk—cut once, and it all breaks at once.
He also said: "With one fist, shatter the barrier of the *pūrvanivāsa*; with one kick, overturn the obstruction of the profound mystery.
Go and come as you please in the four directions; do not seek the Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara. Master Dadian said: "Depart from the four propositions; cut off the hundred negations."
To know that there is no seeing is to arrive at *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, this "non-existence" of *nirvāṇa* does not mean death;
rather, it refers to quiescent extinction (*śānti*), where there is neither birth nor death. The Supreme One says: "Profoundly still and eternally tranquil. The Buddhist sutras say:
"When birth and cessation have ceased, quiescent extinction is bliss. "Quiescent" means still and unmoving; "extinction" means that all phenomena do not arise. In reality, there is no birth.
Death! But tell me: what is the appearance of that which is neither born nor dies? Do not listen for sounds, for they are not the form;
recognize the void, and it is just as it is.
Nirvāṇa is pure and free from right or wrong; It is better to grasp it than to hastily cast away such mad words.
The antics of the fox-like child wander aimlessly and lead to delusion;
The three calamities do not descend from heaven, But are all found by seeking them within oneself.
Abandoning kin for strangers, this man of no talent; Displaying strength, he fails to accord with the Patriarch’s pivot.
The forty-eight vows are not to be treated as weighty; While reciting them with his mouth, his mind and intent are in violation.
The Dharma of non-action has been transmitted from patriarch to patriarch; Yet he takes conditioned action to be the ultimate reality.
All phenomena that possess marks are empty and false; Mud and water mixed together are not the way of the Sugata.
Dragons and snakes entangled in a thousand-fold turmoil— A method that disturbs the nature makes it difficult to reach the ultimate end.
The self was originally non-existent; One must let go further and not be deluded.
On the path to Nirvana there is no companion; on the Great Way there is no self or person—who is it?

As for the Buddhas of the three periods of time: there are one thousand Buddhas of the past Glorious Kalpa, one thousand Buddhas of the future Constellation Kalpa, and one thousand Buddhas of the present Worthy and Holy Kalpa.
These are the three thousand Buddhas of the three periods; are there further Buddhas beyond the limit of kalpas?
It can be spoken of; it cannot be spoken of. Its measure and number are inexhaustible. All these Buddhas have attained this through cultivation and realization.

Master Chuan said: "Plant melons and you get melons; plant fruits and you get fruits. He also said: "One Buddha, two Buddhas, ten thousand or a hundred thousand Buddhas—each has eyes askance and a straight nose.
Because they planted roots of goodness in years past, today they receive their power as before."
The *Daojing* says: "Plant orchids and you shall obtain fragrance; plant millet and you shall obtain grain. By doing good, auspiciousness descends; by doing evil, calamity descends.
Furthermore, the Buddhas of the three periods did not achieve Buddhahood without cultivation. Within the human body, there likewise exist these Buddhas, yet their manifestations are not uniform.
Because they are obscured by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and hindered by objective phenomena, one becomes deluded regarding one's own home and fails to recognize it. If...
To have no mind within the mind is the Buddha of the past. To be tranquil and unmoving is the Buddha of the future.
To respond to conditions and engage with others is the Buddha of the present. To be pure and undefiled is the Stainless Buddha. To enter and exit without obstruction—

To possess spiritual powers is to be the Buddha of Supernatural Penetration; to roam freely everywhere is to be the Buddha of Sovereignty; for the single mind to remain unclouded is to be the Buddha of Radiance;
for the aspiration for the Way to be firm and steadfast is to be the Buddha of Indestructibility. Each and every one of these Buddhas exists within one's own body.

Even if one were to speak, it could not be fully exhausted. Its manifestations are manifold, yet there is only the single Reality. Past, future, and present are all of one and the same substance, like empty space.
It is without differentiated characteristics, without self-characteristics, and without other-characteristics; it is not without characteristics, nor is it a grasped characteristic.
It is not this shore, not the other shore, and not the middle stream. Contemplating its quiescence, it is eternally neither severed nor extinguished. If a person...
Thus awakened suddenly, one directly accepts and takes responsibility for it. The vast reaches of the empty kalpas are entirely present right now. Radiance is emitted and the earth shakes;
both person and phenomena are forgotten. One no longer perceives past, future, or present, ultimately reaching the ground where the finite and the infinite are exhausted.
This is emptiness. Emptiness is the absence of self and the absence of non-self. Since even "self" and "non-self" cannot be found, emptiness and form are likewise non-existent.

The three periods of time are empty by their very nature; it is not that consciousness ceases, but that the nature of consciousness is itself empty. The past, the future, and the present are all empty. Cease clinging to views of emptiness.
Do you truly wish to see the Buddhas of the three periods? *Pah!* Do not continue to suffer from thirst while standing by the river; do not say you are hungry while holding a cake in your hand.
The Buddhas of the three periods fill the vast void;
The subtle differentiation of external forms lies in each and every one being the body of infinite true emptiness. True emptiness envelops both heaven and earth;
In every atom and every land, all are Buddhas, Each and every one radiating brilliance within the mind.
Every person possesses the Tathāgata-mind, yet sentient beings are deluded and distressed, unable to know it.
There are thousands of billions of infinite transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*);
the perfect recompense body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is beyond both good and evil.
The pure Dharma-body is vast and boundless;

If one can awaken to even a fraction of its meaning, One will pierce through heaven and earth and penetrate the profound barrier, Wandering through the three realms yet returning to the original station;
Resting in one's lot and maintaining integrity, one truly suffers no loss.
"There is no Buddha to be made; this is the natural state. By guarding this truth, one's will is fulfilled and the unsurpassed is attained.
This is because one relies upon the Prajñāpāramitā. A practitioner must possess wisdom and a hundredfold skillful means.
One must eliminate habitual tendencies accumulated since beginningless kalpas and harmonize them into the single true nature (*eka-tathatā*) to ascend to the other shore.

If one does not perceive this nature, it will be difficult to achieve success. This phrase is the mother of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; the Buddhas of the ten directions rely upon it for their practice.

When their causal practices are perfected, they attain equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). If one practices apart from this phrase, even after passing through many kalpas, [success will not be attained].
Those who have long maintained their practice with diligent austerity yet rarely succeed in realizing the Great Way are few.

Belonging instead to the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle, they fall into the states of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, ghost-sages, celestial sages, or terrestrial sages—conditioned dharmas that ultimately do not bring about the realization of any holy fruit.
One must therefore apply oneself with vigor; by maintaining the presence of the dharma of Prajñāpāramitā, which transcends both subject and object, one attains the Unconditioned.
The supreme, true Way consists of this one matter alone. Were one to practice otherwise or deviate from this Dharma, such a thing is impossible.
This is the separate transmission outside the teachings; this Dharma is transmitted only after one has personally realized one's own nature. It has not been transmitted by a thousand sages;

it is realized through self-awakening and self-confidence, and no formal prediction (vyākaraṇa) is required. This is the stage of the Perfect and Sudden, a uniquely distinguished teaching. [End of] *Canshenzhijue*.

Consciousness. One must seek out and question the supreme person and rely upon the teacher’s instruction; when there is the karmic affinity for awakening, one realizes it through the Perfect and Sudden Teaching. This teaching transcends human sentiment.
If there is any private intention in its transmission, it is the dharma of external paths. Where there is bestowal, where there is transmission, and where there is gain, there is loss.
There are teachings and there are transmissions; these are all the heterodox views of external paths, the very root of birth and death. The Immortal Master said:
"The Dharma has three thousand six hundred gates, yet one must directly know that there is a subtle and profound place which does not reside within those three thousand six hundred gates.
The Buddhas and Patriarchs, as masters, cultivated and realized it for themselves; originally there were no words or phrases, nor was there a single dharma given to others. If there were..."
The Dharma bestows prediction; it is not called "Śākyamuni," nor is one addressed as a "man of the Way. The Way is fundamentally wordless;

it merely teaches people to cultivate themselves and awaken for themselves. To speak of it is not true. If you are corrupted by others' teachings, you must urgently expel them. Generally speaking, in being a person:
One must cause immeasurable great meaning to flow forth from within oneself, using it without end.

Those of superior capacity awaken to a thousand truths upon hearing it once and possess the Great Dharani. Those of middling and inferior faculties hear much but mostly lack faith. The Supreme One said:

"When the superior person hears the Way, they practice it with diligence; when the middling person hears the Way, they are as if it exists and as if it does not; when the inferior person hears the Way, they laugh at it."
This is a teaching difficult to believe, a rare occurrence.
Because of the *prajñāpāramitā*, each and every one must seek the path for self-exit;
on the boundless Great Way, one penetrates to Chang’an. Let the mind rest at ease and cease all fear.
May one always reach the ultimate goal over vast eons;

With a clear mind, one shall behold Amitāyus and the Buddhas of the three periods gathering at the Dragon Flower Assembly. The Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are beyond calculation;
Faith is itself the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang guo*); Faith is itself the True Pure Land.
In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, may the benevolent deities reverently protect this dwelling place and ensure its peace. May those who are utterly disrespectful,
who turn their backs on their ancestors and forget their kindness, and who do not rely upon the teachings, never behold the Buddhas of the present.
Refuting the heterodox to manifest proof does not conform to worldly sentiments;
it moves all Buddhas because it possesses principle. Cease learning if you are a non-practitioner. Attaining the Way relies entirely upon the assistance of accumulated merit (*yin-zhi*).
"Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" is a Western [Indian] Sanskrit term. *Anuttara* means "without."

*Anuttara* means "unsurpassed" (*an-uttara*). *Samyak* means "thoroughly" (*sam-yañc*). *Sambodhi* means "profound" (*sam-bodhi*). In the Eastern Land [China], this is translated as "Unsurpassed Thorough Profundity.
It is also said to mean "Attaining Equal and Perfect Enlightenment. These four characters must be personally realized. As the ancients said:

"One cultivates the path only after seeing the Way; if one does not see it, what is there to cultivate? Even the entire Tripitaka could not fully explain these four characters. Thus it is with all Buddhas.
This also cannot be fully explained. The sages and worthies of the three teachings all cultivate these four characters;
they all return to the holy path and achieve equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

If people today can practice according to this *prajñāpāramitā*, the dharma of *samyak-saṃbodhi*, they will attain sudden and vast awakening, personally behold the unsurpassed and profound, and know for themselves that they shall become immortals and Buddhas, directly transcending [the mundane].
The fruits of sagehood and the wondrous Way are rooted in the void; their true and responsive manifestations are likewise inexhaustible.
If a person is willing to awaken to the path of true permanence, they will recognize their original lord from of old.
*An-ou* (Anuttara) means "supreme" and signifies the emptiness of non-duality; *Tuo-lo* (Tathā) means "thus," signifying that it alone is the Honored One;
*San-miao* (Samyak) means "perfectly" and carries the sense of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); *Pu-ti* (Bodhi) means the profound principle, the supreme and ultimate essence.
This four-line verse, supremely profound, was established by the Buddha as he circulated in the world to set forth the gateway of the teachings.
The four-line sublime verse is the mother of the Tripiṭaka; It encompasses all practices without exception.
If there is one who understands these four lines clearly, When one dharma is penetrated, ten thousand dharmas are penetrated.
Transcending birth and death, one leaves the realms of suffering; One attains the indestructible diamond body.
The Dharma of leisurely sitting and reclining on the branches; The skill of standing meditation in accordance with one's seat.
Truly an Arhat leaning against walls and relying on pillars; A person who has realized the Way, inhaling and exhaling freely.
Neither defiled nor pure, there is nothing to cultivate or realize; Neither increasing nor decreasing—this is the manifest perfection.
Unborn and undying, the Immeasurable Life, the World-Honored One manifested from within space;
thus one knows that those who practice the Prajñāpāramitā shall, through such cultivation, behold the unsurpassed and most profound Way.

One knows the divine power of the *prajñāpāramitā*. Furthermore, the Buddhas of the past, out of their compassion and pity for sentient beings, employed the power of a hundred kinds of wisdom and skillful means to transform people.
They caused clay, wood, and carved images, as well as yellow scrolls and red axes [of scripture], to speak of causes and effects.
Yet they did so merely by using provisional names to guide sentient beings, employing the matters of karmic retribution for good and evil.
The discourse on heaven and hell is intended to cause people to reform their evils and follow the good, to leave the false and return to the true.
It provides a gradual guidance through the stages of the ten sages and three worthies, as well as the levels of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all Buddhas. The Immortal Master said:

"A journey of a thousand *li* is advanced step by step. The Buddha said: "A jeweled terrace eight thousand cubits high cannot be ascended with a single leap. One must suddenly awaken to it oneself and see it for oneself.
The original nature transcends the stages and ranks of all Buddhas; with a single leap, one enters directly into the stage of the Tathāgata.
If one does not see this nature, but instead runs outward in pursuit, one will never achieve success. Daowu said: "A thousand days of studying the Way, realization occurs in a single moment.
It is in this very moment that one attains lightness and ease; all superior beings return to the same place. As for intellectual understanding, it is merely following the ancients.

These spittle-droppers are all followers of external paths with false views; they wander through the various paths of birth and death, receiving retribution according to their karma, and are not to be spoken with.
Have you not heard how Subhūti practiced for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, until he attained the foremost wisdom in understanding emptiness beneath Śākyamuni’s assembly?
He then requested the four-line verse, whereupon he attained sudden enlightenment in a vast, open space, weeping tears of sorrow and lamenting to himself:
The eye of wisdom previously attained has not yet heard this sutra. All Buddhas of the three periods of time flow forth from this sutra;
what, then, is this sutra? Although it does not contain a single word, it radiates light day and night.
Prajñā is to turn back and reflect; it is to shed the old skin and change the bones to realize non-arising.
It is the answer to the fundamental source;
it is to change one’s body and mind to engage in discourse that is more eloquent and sharp than the ordinary.
The mind becomes clear and lucid, knowing what precedes and follows; there is nothing it does not penetrate.
The heavens open like mist clearing, and drifting clouds retreat.
Radiance appears as if ordinary, while springs well up from the earth and the hundred grasses sprout anew.
The running beasts rejoice, the flying birds are glad;
Wings spread in the air, filling the mountains and rivers. The flowers bloom;
the *pāramitā* that realizes nature and clarifies the mind— Because of this sound, empty space is shattered to pieces.
Behold one’s own mother— this iron-faced skin— is originally unborn,
just like a single red wheel that universally illumines the ten directions throughout the entire dharma-realm, without a single speck of dark cloud.
One thousand seven hundred: the gateways of profound mystery. Each gateway is split open, pervading the entire earth;
The thicket of entanglements is uprooted along with its soil, severing the cycle of rebirth.
Realizing the Golden Body, the work is perfected and the fruit is fulfilled.
Turning the Wheel of Dharma, To rescue and deliver me, Emerging from the weary straits of delusion through countless kalpas,
Practicing austerities with a firm mind that never retreats—
Were it not for this true practice, How would I dare ascend to the celestial palace?
In ordinary beings, it is not originally less;
When one enters the stage of the sages, it does not originally increase. It remains as it was, half a catty;
Originally unborn and originally unextinguished, One falsely gives rise to delusions and inversions.
"Simply turn the light back; if you are willing to reflect inwardly, each and every one will achieve perfect completion—this is the Great Divine Mantra.
It is possessed by all people, yet it is difficult to clarify without cultivation. This divine mantra is also the Dharma-gate of the sentient beings' own mind-ground.
It possesses a great divine path. As it is said: 'When the mind has a sovereign master, ten thousand evils cannot invade. The Confucians say: 'The mind...'"
It is precisely for the purpose of warding off malevolent influences. The *Duren Jing* (Sūtra on Deliverance) states: "Ten thousand evils cannot disturb it; the divine spirits guard its gate.

It can expel the heterodox and establish the orthodox, transform the dead into the living, and change demonic realms into celestial realms. Every single manifestation reveals the truth, and every object fully displays its nature.
When one picks up anything at hand with faith, there is no hindrance whatsoever. This great divine mantra—should one raise a thought or stir a mind—the ghosts and spirits [are subdued].
Extinguishing delusions, one returns to the root and reverts to the source; externalists’ souls are struck with terror, and their spirits cower in concealment. This is the secret mantra.
Wherever supernatural powers and wondrous functions manifest, they follow [the practitioner] everywhere. Possessing great majestic spiritual power, one wields the sword to quell malevolent spirits.
Without departing from the square inch of the heart-mind, those dwelling together do not recognize it.
This great divine mantra possesses efficacious power; Wisdom penetrates every kind and every object.

Without ever opening the mouth, one first awakens to awareness; The nature is like a cold pond, clear to its very bottom— Ineffable and unfathomable is the essence of true emptiness, Manifesting its numinous root through a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes.
The life-vein winds of all Buddhas do not penetrate; One strikes open the true and wondrous gate of the mind-ground.
A single segment of pure emptiness is the Great Principle; Within the body with form lies the formless body— It cannot be captured by a cat, nor can it be painted;
This unconditioned samādhi is difficult even for spirits to clarify.
Majestic and unmoving is the place where the body rests; The Samādhi of Universal Radiance illuminates the essence of demons.
Ordinary and sage dwell together, leaning upon the staff; When demons come to inflict harm, do not comply with their whims.
Within this, there is originally no root or trace; Who in the void dares to forcibly bestow a name?
Casually pointing out the Vajra-eye, it pierces through the eighty thousand leagues of the Demon King;
this is the Great Illuminating Mantra. A single point of spiritual radiance naturally shines forth, penetrating the ten directions and piercing through the three realms.
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth present no obstruction; surpassing the sun and moon, there is nowhere it does not illuminate. As the Ancestor Lü said:
A single spark of the mind’s lamp flares up flame by flame; no need for laborious trimming, it shines with brilliant clarity.

Having attained this, it pierces the darkness of the human world, alone emitting a cold radiance that fills the vast void. The light of Amitābha, the very nature of wood—raising an eyebrow or blinking an eye, it is brilliantly manifest.
Constantly bright day and night without interruption, never obscured at any moment, it appears in the Western Paradise. Lofty and majestic, a single blossom.

A lotus of purple-gold radiates ten thousand beams of light, illuminating the great trichiliocosm. To realize that the Land of Ultimate Bliss manifests in every realm, and to understand that the Pure Land is present before one’s eyes—this is the Great Illuminating Mantra:
"Manifesting the Golden Light," this is the Great Illuminating Mantra: "Illuminating the Ten Directions."
The mind gives rise to brilliance; it shines resplendent and vast.
Rivers, mountains, and seas offer no obstruction.
With the heavenly eye, it illuminates the azure void.
The light is of one essence; at the zenith of heaven, it shines all around without falling into partiality.
While the sun and moon come and go, alternating between brightness and darkness, there is neither light nor darkness—this is the light of one's own self.
The two wheels of sun and moon are the eyes of heaven and earth;
from the first moment of radiance, countless billions of transformation Buddhas appear within the light.
Their infinite bodies are joined as one, and through their spiritual powers they manifest transformations and changes; the principle of the pure Dharma-body is complete.
This unsurpassed mantra allows one to behold the radiance of one's own self, illuminating and revealing the darkness from the past;
there is nothing that can surpass it. This divine mantra is the most supreme, none excels it, and it is the foremost.

All dharmas do not transcend this heart-mantra. Its radiance shines through with clarity, universally illuminating the ten directions, encompassing the entire dharma-realm, and standing alone from antiquity.
"Qian and Kun. Even if one were to employ other divine mantras, they could never surpass this mantra;
it is the unsurpassed mantra. Dao said, "The mind is the king of all. Shi said, "The mind is the king among dharmas. It is simply this one King who remains unmoving.
The myriad people will naturally find peace. If the mind is not disturbed, no evils will arise.
This is the unsurpassed mantra: "A single segment of emptiness" is the unsurpassed mantra; it has never been divided;
it has no north or south, no west or east.
Without above or below; internal and external are the same;
without sun or moon; without darkness or light;
without ordinary beings or sages; without human relations.
Without past or present; without beginning or end;
the Mother of the Prior Heaven; alone most honored;
the Way of the Ultimateless; the Body of the Great Ultimate.
The Great Ultimate (Taiji) originally has the Non-polar (Wuji) as its substance; The Non-polar originally has the Great Ultimate as its root.
From the beginning of the Great Ultimate, the Two Forms (Li-yi) were divided; The clear and the turbid, ascending and descending, are the traces of Heaven and Earth.
Yang comes as the father and Yin as the mother; They gather and form a shape, transforming into human beings.
The transformations of the Three Powers (Heaven, Earth, and Humanity) are inexhaustible; from branch to branch and leaf to leaf, they continue unto this day.
This is the Peerless Mantra (*Asamasama-dhāraṇī*). There is nothing equal to this mantra; it cannot be described and cannot be compared. It has no boundaries.
In this world, it is difficult to believe when this mantra is briefly spoken of; one must personally witness its clarity and realize it for oneself.
This is the mantra. When this mantra is unfolded, it encompasses the vast void; when gathered back, not even a hair’s breadth of a thing can be established.
