This mantra is most profound and most wondrous, most honored and most noble, greatest and deepest. It is the mantra of one’s own mind.
Clearly raised before the seamless stupa, many miss it by failing to penetrate the mysterious pass. A single clear phrase encompasses both the mundane and the sacred.
Within this very midst dwells the Ancient Amitābha; If one did not cultivate it in past lives, one knows it not now. At the profound gate of ten thousand fathoms, travelers are rare.
Should there be anyone who can simply turn toward it with devotion, They will surely realize perfect clarity and become equal to the Buddha.
This peerless mantra is most wondrous; its name resounds as a precious title, shining brilliantly through the vast void.
A single segment of golden light, it illuminates heaven and earth and lights the path through the darkness.
This mantra of infinite and great spiritual power—none of the various other mantras can equal it.
This mantra is the mother of all mantras; With the slightest stir of thought or movement of mind, the mantra manifests.
It encompasses heaven and wraps around earth, *dhāraṇī*;
Spirits and ghosts flee in terror, not daring to deceive.
There is one who, by reciting this efficacious mantra, crushes *chimei* (goblins) so they are transformed into ash,
and likewise destroys *wangliang* (sprites) and malevolent demons.
To those who can eliminate all suffering— those who transform the strange and monstrous, dissolve the hells, and liberate one from the cycle of rebirth—
the Buddhas and Patriarchs appear in the world and employ various skillful means to rescue and deliver all beings.
Deluded ones, come forth together from the court of fire. If there are those possessed of wisdom, listen attentively to the words of the Great Way;
investigate only the ground of the mind and do not seek elsewhere. First, sweep it clean and remove the habitual tendencies accumulated over kalpas. As Dadian said:

When a pond is dug, one does not wait for the moon; once the pond is completed, the moon comes of its own accord. A practitioner of the Way must first purify the mind, and the Way will naturally arise.
The Confucians say: "Regulate the mind with ritual. The Buddhists say: "Dwell in a secluded place and gather the mind within. The Daoists say: "Subdue the mind and sever all thoughts.
The sages of the Three Teachings teach nothing other than making the mind of sentient beings pure and empty. If the mind is without [defilement]...

Tainted by defilements, one naturally fails to see one's nature. If one attains the seeing of one's nature, one will forever escape saṃsāra and no longer undergo rebirth, attaining the Way of neither death nor birth.
Furthermore, the Buddhas and sages of the past underwent long periods of diligent suffering before they finally attained the seeing of their nature;
yet, in every thought and every moment, they encountered it everywhere. But tell me, where does it go at the very end? If you do not realize it, it is everywhere.
The path of delusion returns; awakening reveals that from the start one was always in one’s own native land.
Being able to eliminate all suffering, one is then free from it; transcending the three realms and escaping the three miserable paths;
for the sake of the Dharma, forgetting the body and departing from the five desires.
The body of true gold is refined through the five turbidities;
the five precepts are inviolable and difficult to govern;
there is neither merit nor transgression, for it is beyond the five punishments.
Within the emptiness of the five aggregates, there is neither ordinary person nor sage;
To never lack the five constants is to possess great virtue.
Worldly affairs are in a frantic rush with no end in sight; The burning house is in a state of panic, yet suffering remains unrecognized.
If you once again believe and accept the words of the Buddhas, The fire pit will transform into a pond of white lotuses;
In this defiled land, this turbid world of suffering Saha, Where since beginningless time much karma has been created,
By clarifying the essence and returning to the realization of perfect emptiness, One turns the body around and leaps out of the nest of birth and death.
"True and not false" means this is the Dharma-discourse of reality; it is not empty or flowery speech.
All Buddhas have spoken this mantra to deliver sentient beings; it is not a divergent word, nor is it a humble statement. Yongjia said: "Realize the true mark."
The dharma of non-self; the momentary extinction of karma. All that possesses marks is entirely false; only this markless mark is the true mark.
When the great trichiliocosm is utterly destroyed, this mark is not destroyed. Why is it not destroyed? A Way-sayer said: "That which has form is ultimately false;
the markless is the True Person. It is further said: "When the hundred bones have all dissolved..."

Scattered. A single object eternally presides over the numinous. The *Duren Jing* (Scripture of Saving Humanity), a Daoist scripture, states: "The Original Beginning suspended a precious pearl (as large as a millet grain) within the profound void."
A Buddhist sutra says: "I have a priceless jewel tied within my garment; though I have searched for it day and night, I suddenly behold the Muni-jewel.
It further says: "The Muni-jewel is unrecognized by men, yet it is personally held within the Tathāgatagarbha.
Although this is so, while seeing the Way may be easy, guarding the Way is difficult. Do you wish to see this jewel? It is perfectly round and its radiance is brilliantly shining.
Whirling and turning, lively and vibrant, ever facing one, yet ungraspable.
This true and unfailing flow of the Buddha’s grace directly points to the four dhāraṇīs, teaching people the infinite Way that pervades heaven and earth.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, it moves freely in all ways.
My teacher was not yet enlightened, so it was difficult to enter the principle; Without receiving the true transmission, there was nowhere to turn for refuge.
Having endured thirteen years of hardship, I cast aside all dharmas and did not harbor them in my mind.
Holding up emptiness without letting go, The boundless realms were entirely penetrated.
Within emptiness upon emptiness, there is still a place that is not empty; True Emptiness is fundamentally the ancient family style—
the indestructible body,
the root of all sages.
"Knowing that by turning away from [delusion] one returns to the original ground, and because the lamps are transmitted in succession with equal brightness, it is called the Prajñāpāramitā Dhāraṇī.
This is because, through the practice of cultivation, one reaches this point and comes to know the efficacy of Prajñā.
"Most capable, most supreme, and greatest. This phrase concludes the various aforementioned expedient means. Possessing great *dhāraṇī*, all things return to the single mind.
As the ancients said: "One should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm; all is created by the mind alone. The Immortal Zhen said:
"Good and evil, existence and non-existence, all reside within the mind. Da Dian said: "The deluded become the *ālayavijñāna*; after death, they become venomous snakes. The awakened..."
This is a secret divine mantra. One attains the dharma of non-arising. The Tathāgata has this esoteric teaching, which Kāśyapa does not conceal.

If a person single-mindedly receives and maintains this divine mantra, their meritorious practice will reach fulfillment. By constantly holding this mantra, ghosts and spirits will keep their distance.
The various devas listen in silence, ever filled with joy.
Prajñā is vast, wisdom is expansive, spiritual powers are great,
the ocean is deep, and transformations are inexhaustible.
Profound and wondrous, immeasurable and unfathomable;
pure and tranquil, without a speck of dust;
having reached the other shore, one guards the truth and fulfills the vow.
Truly, one attains the vision of non-arising;
